title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Where we are

Sessions 3–4: the outcome is spatially clustered, and we know where
Today: regression on areas. The usual assumption of independent residuals often fails
By the end you can:

test regression residuals for spatial autocorrelation
use Lagrange multiplier tests to choose lag or error
fit and compare spatial lag and spatial error models
report a spatial analysis

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Fit OLS first

ols <- lm(dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct, data = blocks)
round(summary(ols)$coefficients, 3)

              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   -101.067     61.802  -1.635    0.106
poverty_index    1.445      0.335   4.306    0.000
literacy_pct     0.981      0.603   1.629    0.107

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Moran’s I on the residuals

lm.morantest(ols, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)


    Global Moran I for regression residuals

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
weights: lw

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 4.4335, p-value = 4.635e-06
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Observed Moran I      Expectation         Variance 
     0.273945405     -0.023128244      0.004489825 



A significant positive residual Moran’s I means the model leaves spatial structure unexplained: independence fails and standard errors are probably too small.


blocks$res_ols <- residuals(ols)
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = res_ols)) + scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", name = "Residual") +
  labs(title = "OLS residuals: neighbours share the same sign")

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Two structures








Model
Idea
Think of




Spatial lag (SAR)
my outcome depends on my neighbours’ outcomes
contagion, spillover


Spatial error (SEM)
omitted shared factors make neighbouring errors alike
unmeasured exposures




Lag: y = ρWy + Xβ + ε   |   Error: y = Xβ + u, u = λWu + ε

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Choosing from the LM tests

If only one plain test is significant, use that model
If both are, prefer the model whose robust test (adjRSerr or adjRSlag) is larger and significant
Use theory too: contagion points to lag, omitted exposures to error

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Fit and compare

sem <- errorsarlm(dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct, data = blocks, listw = lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
sar <- lagsarlm(dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct, data = blocks, listw = lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
c(lambda = sem$lambda, rho = sar$rho) |> round(3)

lambda.lambda       rho.rho 
        0.535         0.515 

AIC(ols, sem, sar)

    df      AIC
ols  4 698.4286
sem  5 687.2759
sar  5 684.6838



c(OLS = unname(moran.test(residuals(ols), lw, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1]), SEM = unname(moran.test(residuals(sem), lw, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1])) |> round(3)

   OLS    SEM 
 0.274 -0.042 


Lower AIC is better (same data). The residual Moran’s I should fall towards 0.

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Coefficients in the lag model

In a lag model a change in one block’s poverty also changes its neighbours’ rates, which feed back. The coefficient is not the whole effect. Report impacts: direct, indirect and total.


set.seed(6)
summary(impacts(sar, listw = lw, R = 199), zstats = TRUE, short = TRUE)

Impact measures (lag, exact):
                       Direct  Indirect    Total
poverty_index dy/dx 0.9339023 0.8647157 1.798618
literacy_pct dy/dx  0.8134276 0.7531661 1.566594
========================================================
Simulation results ( variance matrix):
========================================================
Simulated standard errors
                       Direct  Indirect     Total
poverty_index dy/dx 0.3400153 0.5790857 0.7998079
literacy_pct dy/dx  0.6010227 0.8975023 1.4072140

Simulated z-values:
                      Direct  Indirect    Total
poverty_index dy/dx 2.715598 1.5611009 2.284744
literacy_pct dy/dx  1.332292 0.9089538 1.148742

Simulated p-values:
                    Direct    Indirect Total   
poverty_index dy/dx 0.0066156 0.11850  0.022328
literacy_pct dy/dx  0.1827641 0.36337  0.250662


In the error model the coefficients keep the OLS meaning, with corrected standard errors.

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Other routes

Add covariates that explain the clustering; the residual autocorrelation may vanish
Count data with unequal populations: Poisson models with a spatial random effect (CAR / BYM in INLA, brms)
Geographically weighted regression lets coefficients vary over space
Always map the residuals

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Reporting checklist


The outcome (rate, not count) and the areas, with the CRS if distances were used
The weights: definition, standardisation, isolates
Global result: Moran’s I, p-value type, simulations
Local results: method, adjustment, map; say they are exploratory
Regression: residual Moran’s I, LM tests, model chosen and why, parameter (rho or lambda), AIC vs OLS, impacts for a lag model
Limitations: area size (MAUP), small numbers, edge effects, association not cause

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (1/5)

Residuals of an area-level regression have a significant positive Moran’s I. What is the main consequence?

The regression coefficients become zero in each of the fitted models
The model must be refitted using fewer of the areas in the data
Standard errors are probably too small, so p-values are optimistic
The outcome variable is spatially random and so should be dropped

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

Which situation points to a spatial LAG model?

An unmeasured exposure affects blocks that lie next to each other
The outcome in an area influences its neighbours’ outcomes (contagion)
The residuals are normally distributed with a constant variance throughout
The covariates are strongly correlated with each other and with the outcome

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

Both plain LM tests are significant, but only the robust lag test is. What do you conclude?

A spatial error model is the better candidate
Neither model is needed, so ordinary regression is fine
A spatial lag model is the better candidate
The tests are contradictory, so they should be ignored

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

In a spatial lag model, why is the coefficient of a covariate not its full effect?

The coefficient is divided by the number of areas in the study
Lag models estimate the effects for the neighbours, not for the area
The coefficient is measured on a different scale from the outcome
A change in one area also changes its neighbours’ outcomes

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Self-check quiz (5/5)

After fitting a spatial error model, what should you check?

The residual Moran’s I, which should now be close to 0
Whether the number of blocks has doubled during fitting
That each covariate has become significant at the 5% level
Whether the lambda value has become equal to 1

title: Session 5 — Spatial Regression and Reporting
text:
Score and take-home
Your score: 

Always test residuals of an area-level regression (lm.morantest)
LM tests (and robust versions) suggest lag or error; theory should agree
Report rho / lambda, AIC vs OLS, the residual check; use impacts for lag
For counts with unequal populations, consider Poisson models with spatial random effects

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Where we are

Sessions 1–2: spatial data, maps, neighbours and weights
Today: is the pattern clustered? One test for the whole map
By the end you can:

compute and interpret Moran’s I, with analytic and permutation p-values
read the Moran scatterplot
choose between Moran’s I, Geary’s C, General G and join counts
report a global result in one sentence

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Are similar values neighbours?

I = ( n / Σ wij ) × ΣiΣj wij (xi − x̄)(xj − x̄) / Σi (xi − x̄)²


Multiply each area’s deviation from the mean by its neighbours’ average deviation (the lag), then scale by the variance
High areas with high neighbours, low with low → products positive → I > 0
Expectation with no pattern: E[I] = −1/(n−1), about 0




I
Meaning




≈ 0
no spatial pattern


clearly > 0
clustering: similar values are neighbours


clearly < 0
dispersion: neighbours differ (a checkerboard; rare)

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Four areas by hand

v <- c(1, 2, 9, 10)
nb4 <- list(2L, c(1L, 3L), c(2L, 4L), 3L); class(nb4) <- "nb"; attr(nb4, "region.id") <- as.character(1:4)
lw4 <- nb2listw(nb4, style = "W"); z <- v - mean(v)
c(by_hand = (4 / sum(unlist(lw4$weights))) * sum(z * lag.listw(lw4, z)) / sum(z^2), moran_test = unname(moran.test(v, lw4)$estimate[1]))

   by_hand moran_test 
 0.5384615  0.5384615 


The two large values sit next to each other, so I is strongly positive. The function and the formula agree.

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
On the district

mi <- moran.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
mi


    Moran I test under randomisation

data:  blocks$dengue_per_100k  
weights: lw    

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 7.4403, p-value = 5.025e-14
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
      0.499247498      -0.012820513       0.004736744 



Read it from the bottom: observed I (about 0.5), its expectation (about 0), and the z-score and p-value. Strong positive spatial autocorrelation.

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
The permutation (Monte Carlo) test
Shuffle the values over the areas 999 times; how often does a shuffled map beat the real I?

set.seed(1)
mc <- moran.mc(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, nsim = 999, zero.policy = TRUE)
ggplot(tibble(I = mc$res[-length(mc$res)]), aes(I)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mc$statistic, colour = col_red, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Moran's I of shuffled maps", title = paste0("Observed I (red) vs 999 shuffles: p = ", mc$p.value))



Assumption-light; usually the better p-value to report
With 999 shuffles the smallest p is 0.001

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text: The permutation (Monte Carlo) test

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
section: Value against the average of its neighbours
text:
Value against the average of its neighbours

blocks$z <- as.numeric(scale(blocks$dengue_per_100k)); blocks$lag_z <- lag.listw(lw, blocks$z, zero.policy = TRUE)
ggplot(blocks, aes(z, lag_z)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = high_burden), size = 2.4) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black") +
  annotate("text", x = c(2.2, -2.2, 2.2, -2.2), y = c(2.2, -2.2, -2.2, 2.2), label = c("High-High", "Low-Low", "High-Low", "Low-High"), colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Rate (standardised)", y = "Neighbours' average (standardised)", colour = NULL)



The slope of the line is Moran’s I (here 0.5)
High-High / Low-Low points make positive autocorrelation
High-Low / Low-High points are spatial outliers: LISA (Session 4) finds them

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
section: Value against the average of its neighbours
text: Value against the average of its neighbours

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Which global test?









Test
Question
Variable
Reading




Moran’s I
Are similar values neighbours?
continuous
I > E[I]: clustering


Geary’s C
Are neighbours’ differences small?
continuous
C < 1 clustering (opposite of I)


General G
Do high or low values cluster?
continuous, positive
G > E[G]: highs cluster


Join counts
Do same-category areas touch?
binary / categorical
more same-category joins than expected

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
section: Geary’s C, General G, join counts
text:
Geary’s C, General G, join counts

geary.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate

Geary C statistic       Expectation          Variance 
      0.466797918       1.000000000       0.004855649 

lw_b <- nb2listw(nb, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
globalG.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw_b, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate

Global G statistic        Expectation           Variance 
      7.320125e-02       6.718598e-02       3.916081e-06 

joincount.test(blocks$high_burden, lw_b, zero.policy = TRUE)[[2]]$estimate

Same colour statistic           Expectation              Variance 
             39.00000              18.54333              10.97242 



Moran’s I is positive for both hot-spot and cold-spot clustering. Only General G says whether the high values are the ones that cluster. Join counts suit a yes/no variable.

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Pitfalls


Not saying which weights; not saying which variable (counts and rates differ)
Small areas give noisy rates, which hides or mimics clustering (smooth with empirical Bayes)
Edge effects and the modifiable areal unit problem: a different grouping can change I
A trend (north-south gradient) also gives positive I
A global test cannot say where; a non-significant I can hide a local cluster

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
How to report

Dengue incidence was strongly clustered across the 79 blocks (global Moran’s I = 0.50, queen contiguity, row-standardised weights; permutation p = 0.001, 999 simulations).

Give the statistic, the weights, the number of simulations and the p-value; then say where, with local methods.

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Self-check quiz (1/5)

Global Moran’s I is 0.49 (permutation p = 0.001). What is the best interpretation?

49% of the variation in the rate is explained by the location
Each area’s rate is 0.49 higher than its neighbours’ average rate
Neighbouring areas are more alike than expected by chance
About half of all the areas lie in a significant local cluster

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

What is the expected value of Moran’s I when there is no spatial pattern?

Exactly 1, because every area is its own neighbour
About 0 (exactly −1/(n−1))
Exactly 0.5, halfway between the two extremes
It depends on the data, so there is no expected value

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

With 999 permutations, what is the smallest possible p-value from moran.mc()?

0, if the observed I is larger than every one of the shuffled values
0.05, which is the usual cut-off used for a significant result
0.001, as the observed value is one of 1000 arrangements
It varies from one data set to another and has no fixed minimum

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

Geary’s C is 0.47. How should this be read?

Neighbours differ strongly, so negative spatial autocorrelation
There is no spatial pattern, because C is not equal to zero
The result is invalid, because C must lie between 0 and 1
Neighbours are similar, so positive spatial autocorrelation

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Self-check quiz (5/5)

Moran’s I is positive and significant. What does the General G test add?

Whether high values (hot spots) or low values cluster
The exact location of each separate cluster on the map
A correction of the p-value for the multiple testing
Nothing, because it always gives the same answer as Moran’s I

title: Session 3 — Global Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
Score and take-home
Your score: 

Moran’s I: are similar values neighbours? Compare with about 0
Prefer the permutation p-value; always give the weights
The Moran scatterplot shows slope = I and the four quadrants
Geary’s C (1 = none), General G (hot vs cold), join counts (binary)

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Where we are

Health data has a place: a village, a block, a facility, a patient’s home
Today: how R stores places, and how to make an honest map
By the end you can:

read spatial data and say what an sf object is
name the CRS and transform before measuring
join attributes and spatially join points to polygons
map rates, not counts, with a defensible classification

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Our data: a synthetic district



79 blocks (polygons) with population, poverty, literacy, dengue cases
30 health facilities (points)
Everything is invented: no real boundaries or people
Built so dengue clusters in space: later sessions test that

text:
Three kinds of vector geometry (plus raster)



Type
Example
Class




Point
facility, case home
POINT

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
section: A CRS says how numbers become places
text:
A CRS says how numbers become places


Geographic (e.g. EPSG:4326)

longitude / latitude in degrees
good for storing and web maps
wrong for area and distance


Projected (e.g. UTM 44N, EPSG:32644)

metres
good for area, length, distance, buffers
one projection suits one region



st_crs(blocks)$input

[1] "WGS 84"

blocks_utm <- st_transform(blocks, 32644)
st_crs(blocks_utm)$input

[1] "EPSG:32644"

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Why it matters

tibble(block = blocks$block_id[1:3], recorded_km2 = blocks$area_km2[1:3],
       computed_in_metres = round(as.numeric(st_area(blocks_utm))[1:3] / 1e6, 1))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  block recorded_km2 computed_in_metres
  <chr>        <dbl>              <dbl>
1 B01           71.8               71.8
2 B02           97.7               97.7
3 B03           65.8               65.8



Always check st_crs() before measuring. Two layers can only be combined if they share a CRS, so st_transform() one to match the other.

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Attribute join and spatial join

fac <- read_csv(fac_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |> st_as_sf(coords = c("easting_m", "northing_m"), crs = 32644)
blocks_utm$n_fac <- lengths(st_intersects(blocks_utm, fac))     # facilities per block
table(blocks_utm$n_fac)


 0  1  2  3 
54 21  3  1 



Attribute join: left_join(sf_object, table, by = "key"): same as ordinary data
Spatial join: st_join(points, polygons): which polygon is each point in?
st_intersects() / st_within() give TRUE/FALSE per pair; lengths() counts them
st_distance() gives distances in the CRS units (metres if projected)

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Distance to the nearest facility

cen <- st_centroid(blocks_utm)
blocks_utm$km_to_fac <- apply(st_distance(cen, fac), 1, min) / 1000
ggplot(blocks_utm) + geom_sf(aes(fill = km_to_fac)) + geom_sf(data = fac, colour = "red", size = 1.6) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "km", direction = -1) + labs(title = "Distance to nearest facility (red = facilities)")

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Counts mislead, rates do not

p1 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_cases)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Cases") + labs(title = "Counts")
p2 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "per 100,000", option = "magma", direction = -1) + labs(title = "Rate per 100,000")
p1 + p2



Counts follow population size. Map rates for risk; counts only for workload.

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text: Counts mislead, rates do not

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Classification changes the story

library(classInt)
cls <- function(x, style) cut(x, classIntervals(x, 5, style = style)$brks, include.lowest = TRUE)
bind_rows(mutate(blocks, scheme = "Equal interval", k = cls(dengue_per_100k, "equal")),
          mutate(blocks, scheme = "Quantile", k = cls(dengue_per_100k, "quantile")),
          mutate(blocks, scheme = "Jenks", k = cls(dengue_per_100k, "jenks"))) |>
  ggplot() + geom_sf(aes(fill = k), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + facet_wrap(~ scheme) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "YlOrRd", name = NULL) + theme_void(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")



Equal interval: honest about scale, but a skewed variable crowds one class
Quantile: always shows a “worst 20%” even if all areas are similar
Jenks: groups similar values, but breaks change with the data
State the scheme and breaks; keep them fixed to compare maps

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text: Classification changes the story

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Colour

Sequential (light to dark) for rates
Diverging only around a meaningful midpoint (e.g. rate ratio = 1)
No rainbow; viridis and ColorBrewer are colour-blind safe
A good map has a title, legend with units, source (and scale bar / north arrow when area matters)

Self-check quiz (1/5)

Why must a layer be transformed to a projected CRS before you call st_area() or st_distance()?

The functions will not run on a layer that is stored in degrees
Projected systems store more digits, so the answers are more precise
A degree covers a different ground distance at different latitudes
Distances in metres are needed only when you want to draw a map

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Self-check quiz (2/5)

A district map shows dengue CASES by block, and the largest blocks look worst. What is the best fix?

Switch to a darker colour scale so that the differences stand out more clearly
Map cases per 100,000 people so different block sizes compare fairly
Remove the blocks that have the largest populations from the map entirely
Use quantile classes so that the very worst blocks are not shown at all

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Self-check quiz (3/5)

You have a table of facilities with columns easting_m and northing_m, in UTM zone 44N. What must you give st_as_sf() besides the coordinate columns?

The number of facilities, to allocate the geometry column
A polygon layer, because points need an area to sit in
The CRS, so R knows how the numbers map to places
Nothing else, since R can guess the system from the numbers

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Self-check quiz (4/5)

Which statement about classification of a choropleth is correct?

Equal-interval classes put the same number of areas in each class
Natural breaks give identical classes whichever data are being mapped
The scheme that is chosen has no influence on how the map pattern looks
Quantile classes show a worst group, even if all areas are similar

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Self-check quiz (5/5)

What does st_join(points, polygons) return?

The points, each with the attributes of the polygon it falls in
The polygons, each with a count of the points that fall inside them
A single geometry made by merging all of the points and polygons
The distances between each point and each one of the polygons

title: Session 1 — Spatial Data and Maps
text:
Score and take-home
Your score: 

An sf object = data frame + geometry
Check st_crs(); transform to a projected CRS to measure
Attribute joins use keys; spatial joins use location
Map rates; state the classification; use sequential colour

Next: Session 2: neighbours and spatial weights

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text: Every spatial test in this track asks “are neighbouring areas more alike than chance?”. The word neighbour needs a definition first. That definition is the spatial weights matrix, and it is the most influential choice you make.

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Contiguity neighbours
Two polygons are neighbours if they share a boundary:

Rook: share an edge.
Queen: share an edge or a corner (usual default).


nb_q <- poly2nb(blocks, queen = TRUE,  snap = 1e-4)
nb_r <- poly2nb(blocks, queen = FALSE, snap = 1e-4)
summary(nb_q)

Neighbour list object:
Number of regions: 79 
Number of nonzero links: 414 
Percentage nonzero weights: 6.633552 
Average number of links: 5.240506 
Link number distribution:

 2  3  4  5  6  7  8 
 1  7 13 20 28  9  1 
1 least connected region:
3 with 2 links
1 most connected region:
24 with 8 links

c(queen_links = sum(card(nb_q)), rook_links = sum(card(nb_r)))

queen_links  rook_links 
        414         414 



cen <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(blocks))
plot(st_geometry(blocks), border = "grey70", main = "Queen contiguity: links between neighbouring blocks")
plot(nb_q, cen, add = TRUE, col = "red", pch = 19, cex = 0.4)








Check three things in the summary: the average number of neighbours (here about 5), the least and most connected areas, and any isolates (areas with no neighbours, which break many tests unless you use zero.policy = TRUE).

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Distance-based and k-nearest neighbours
When areas are unequal in size, or are points, use distances between centroids:

knn5 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(cen, k = 5))                  # always exactly 5 neighbours
d <- unlist(nbdists(knn2nb(knearneigh(cen, k = 1)), cen))
nb_d <- dnearneigh(cen, 0, max(d))                      # everyone within the smallest distance that links all areas
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(st_geometry(blocks), border = "grey80", main = "5 nearest neighbours"); plot(knn5, cen, add = TRUE, col = "blue", pch = 19, cex = 0.3)
plot(st_geometry(blocks), border = "grey80", main = "Distance band"); plot(nb_d, cen, add = TRUE, col = "darkgreen", pch = 19, cex = 0.3)

















Definition
Neighbours per area
Good for
Watch out for




Queen / rook
varies
polygons of similar size
islands (isolates); big areas have many neighbours


k nearest
exactly k
unequal areas, points
links across a gap or border that are not real


Distance band
varies
points, catchment ideas
too short leaves isolates; too long links everything

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
From neighbours to weights
A neighbour list says who; weights say how much. Styles in nb2listw():

"B" binary: 1 for every neighbour.
"W" row-standardised: each area’s weights sum to 1, so a neighbour’s influence is shared out. The usual choice.
"S" variance-stabilising.


lw <- nb2listw(nb_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
lw$weights[[1]]           # the first block's weights: 1/(number of neighbours) each

[1] 0.25 0.25 0.25 0.25

sum(lw$weights[[1]])

[1] 1

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
The spatial lag
The spatial lag of a variable is the weighted average of the neighbours’ values. With row-standardised weights it is simply “the average of my neighbours”:

blocks$lag_rate <- lag.listw(lw, blocks$dengue_per_100k, zero.policy = TRUE)
blocks |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(block_id, dengue_per_100k, lag_rate) |> head(5) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1)))

  block_id dengue_per_100k lag_rate
1      B01            53.7     27.8
2      B02            31.0     44.9
3      B03            93.6     47.3
4      B04            30.5     35.7
5      B05            57.6     48.7

# check block 1 by hand:
mean(blocks$dengue_per_100k[nb_q[[1]]])

[1] 27.825



patchwork::wrap_plots(
  ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = "Rate") + labs(title = "Rate"),
  ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = lag_rate)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = "Lag") + labs(title = "Spatial lag (neighbours' average)"))








The lag is smoother than the original. The Moran’s I statistic on the next page is essentially the slope of the lag against the value.

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
The choice matters

w_list <- list(queen = nb2listw(nb_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE),
               rook  = nb2listw(nb_r, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE),
               knn5  = nb2listw(knn5, style = "W"),
               distance = nb2listw(nb_d, style = "W"))
map_dfr(w_list, \(w) { m <- moran.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, w, zero.policy = TRUE); tibble(I = unname(m$estimate[1]), p = m$p.value) }, .id = "weights") |>
  mutate(I = round(I, 3), p = signif(p, 2))

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  weights      I        p
  <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 queen    0.499 5   e-14
2 rook     0.499 5   e-14
3 knn5     0.511 1.80e-15
4 distance 0.543 1   e- 9


The conclusion is similar here because the clustering is strong, but with a weak pattern the answer can change with the weights. State your weights, justify them with the biology (how far does a mosquito or a person travel?) and check sensitivity.

title: Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Take-home

A weights matrix turns “near” into numbers; choose it deliberately (queen for polygons, k-nearest or distance for points).
Row-standardised weights make the spatial lag the average of neighbours.
Look for isolates and areas with very many neighbours; report your choice and test the sensitivity.
Next: Global Moran’s I.

title: Spatial Data with sf
text: This page introduces vector spatial data in R with the sf package, using a synthetic district of 79 blocks (data/gis/district_blocks.geojson) and 30 health facilities (data/gis/facilities.csv). The boundaries and numbers are invented; the district was built so that dengue incidence clusters in space, which the later pages exploit. gis/make_gis_data.R regenerates it.

title: Spatial Data with sf
text:
What is spatial data?



Type
Example
In R




Points
health facility, a case’s home
sf (POINT)


Lines
road, river
sf (LINESTRING)


Polygons
block, district, catchment area
sf (POLYGON)


Raster
population grid, satellite image
terra / stars



An sf object is a data frame with one extra column, geometry. All the dplyr verbs you already know work on it.

Read and look

title: Spatial Data with sf
text:
Coordinate reference systems (CRS)
A CRS says how numbers become places. Two families matter:

Geographic (longitude/latitude, e.g. EPSG:4326, WGS 84): units are degrees. Good for storing and web maps, wrong for distances and areas.
Projected (metres, e.g. a UTM zone, EPSG:32644 for 78°E to 84°E in the northern hemisphere): good for area, length, distance and buffers.


st_crs(blocks)$input            # stored in longitude / latitude

[1] "WGS 84"

blocks_utm <- st_transform(blocks, 32644)
st_crs(blocks_utm)$input

[1] "EPSG:32644"








Warning



Always check the CRS before measuring. st_area() on degrees gives meaningless numbers. Transform to a projected CRS first. Two layers can only be combined when they share a CRS.



tibble(block = blocks_utm$block_id[1:3],
       area_km2_recorded = blocks_utm$area_km2[1:3],
       area_km2_computed = round(as.numeric(st_area(blocks_utm))[1:3] / 1e6, 1))

Joining attributes to polygons
A normal data join works, as long as you join onto the sf object (or sf keeps the geometry only on the left side):

text:
Writing spatial data

st_write(blocks_utm, "blocks_utm.gpkg")      # GeoPackage: one file, any CRS, recommended
st_write(blocks, "blocks.geojson")           # GeoJSON: text, web friendly, longitude/latitude
st_write(blocks, "blocks.shp")               # Shapefile: still common; 10-character column names!

title: Spatial Data with sf
text:
Take-home

An sf object is a data frame plus a geometry column; use st_read() and st_write().
Check st_crs() before every analysis; transform to a projected CRS (here EPSG:32644) to measure.
Joins on attributes use left_join(); joins on where things are use st_join() and st_intersects().
Next: Maps and Choropleths.

title: Global Moran’s I
text: Moran’s I is the standard test for spatial autocorrelation: are areas with high values next to other high areas, and low next to low, more often than chance would give? (“Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.”) It answers one global question for the whole map. Where the clusters are is the job of local Moran’s I.

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
The idea in four areas
Four areas in a row, neighbours = the adjacent ones. Values: 1, 2, 9, 10.

v <- c(1, 2, 9, 10)
nb4 <- list(2L, c(1L, 3L), c(2L, 4L), 3L); class(nb4) <- "nb"; attr(nb4, "region.id") <- as.character(1:4)
lw4 <- nb2listw(nb4, style = "W")
z <- v - mean(v)
I_hand <- (length(v) / sum(unlist(lw4$weights))) * sum(z * lag.listw(lw4, z)) / sum(z^2)
c(by_hand = I_hand, moran_test = unname(moran.test(v, lw4)$estimate[1]))

   by_hand moran_test 
 0.5384615  0.5384615 


\[ I \;=\; \frac{n}{\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}}\;\frac{\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}\,(x_i-\bar x)(x_j-\bar x)}{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2} \]
In words: multiply each area’s deviation from the mean by the average deviation of its neighbours (the lag), add up, and scale by the variance. If high areas have high neighbours the products are positive, so \(I>0\). The two big values sit together, so \(I\) is large and positive.







\(I\)
Meaning




near \(E[I] = -1/(n-1)\) (≈ 0)
no spatial pattern (random)


clearly > 0
positive autocorrelation: similar values cluster


clearly < 0
negative: neighbours differ, like a checkerboard (rare in health data)



\(I\) is not a correlation coefficient, but with row-standardised weights it is usually between about −1 and +1. It is the slope of the spatial lag on the value (see the scatterplot below).

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
Run it on the district

mi <- moran.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
mi


    Moran I test under randomisation

data:  blocks$dengue_per_100k  
weights: lw    

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 7.4403, p-value = 5.025e-14
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
      0.499247498      -0.012820513       0.004736744 


Read the output from the bottom: Moran I statistic (observed I), Expectation (what I would be with no pattern), Variance, and the z-score and p-value from the normal approximation. Here I is about 0.5 against an expectation near 0, with a tiny p-value: strong positive spatial autocorrelation.

A permutation (Monte Carlo) p-value
The normal approximation assumes things about the data. The permutation test shuffles the values over the areas many times and asks how often a shuffled map has an I as large as the real one. It is assumption-light and usually the better report.

set.seed(1)
mc <- moran.mc(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, nsim = 999, zero.policy = TRUE)
mc


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  blocks$dengue_per_100k 
weights: lw  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.49925, observed rank = 1000, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater



ggplot(tibble(I = mc$res[-length(mc$res)]), aes(I)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mc$statistic, colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Moran's I of shuffled maps", y = "Count", title = "The observed I (red) against 999 random maps")








The smallest possible one-sided p-value with 999 shuffles is 1/1000 = 0.001.

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
The Moran scatterplot
Plot each area’s value (standardised) against its spatial lag (the average of its neighbours, standardised). The slope of the line is Moran’s I.

blocks$z <- as.numeric(scale(blocks$dengue_per_100k))
blocks$lag_z <- lag.listw(lw, blocks$z, zero.policy = TRUE)
ggplot(blocks, aes(z, lag_z)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = high_burden), size = 2.2) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = c(2.2, -2.2, 2.2, -2.2), y = c(2.2, -2.2, -2.2, 2.2), label = c("High-High", "Low-Low", "High-Low", "Low-High"), colour = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Dengue rate (standardised)", y = "Average of neighbours (standardised)", colour = "Block burden",
       title = "Moran scatterplot") 







coef(lm(lag_z ~ z, data = blocks))[["z"]] |> round(3)

[1] 0.499



High-High (top right) and Low-Low (bottom left) points create positive autocorrelation.
High-Low and Low-High points are spatial outliers: they differ from their surroundings. They are what LISA will flag.

title: Global Moran’s I
section: Does it depend on how you count?
text:
Does it depend on how you count?

set.seed(2)
tibble(variable = c("Dengue per 100,000", "Dengue cases (counts)", "Poverty index", "Literacy (%)", "Population"),
       x = list(blocks$dengue_per_100k, blocks$dengue_cases, blocks$poverty_index, blocks$literacy_pct, blocks$population)) |>
  mutate(res = map(x, \(v) moran.mc(v, lw, nsim = 999, zero.policy = TRUE)),
         I = map_dbl(res, "statistic"), p = map_dbl(res, "p.value")) |>
  select(variable, I, p) |> mutate(I = round(I, 2))

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  variable                  I     p
  <chr>                 <dbl> <dbl>
1 Dengue per 100,000     0.5  0.001
2 Dengue cases (counts)  0.3  0.001
3 Poverty index          0.75 0.001
4 Literacy (%)           0.53 0.001
5 Population            -0.01 0.48 


Poverty is spatially smooth; population is a random draw per block and shows nothing. Always say which variable and which weights you tested.

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
Pitfalls

Weights choice: repeat with another neighbour definition (page).
Rates with small populations are noisy. Unstable rates in small areas weaken or mimic clustering. For small-area rates, smooth them first (empirical Bayes: EBImoran.mc()).
Edge effects: areas on the border have fewer neighbours, because the study region is cut off.
The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP): the same people grouped into different areas can give different values of I.
One number for the whole map. A significant I does not say where the clusters are, and a non-significant I can hide a strong local cluster.
Association, not cause. Clustering suggests shared exposures (or contagion), it does not identify them.
Trend is not clustering. A smooth north-south gradient also gives positive I; if you suspect a trend, model it and test the residuals (regression page).

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
How to report it

Dengue incidence was strongly clustered across the 79 blocks (global Moran’s I = 0.50, queen-contiguity weights, row-standardised; permutation p = 0.001 with 999 simulations).

Give the statistic, the weights, the number of simulations and the p-value; follow with local analysis to say where.

title: Global Moran’s I
text:
Take-home

Moran’s I tests whether similar values are neighbours; compare it with its expectation of about 0.
Prefer the permutation p-value and always state the weights.
The Moran scatterplot shows the slope and the High-High, Low-Low, High-Low and Low-High groups.
A global test cannot locate clusters: next, Local Moran’s I (LISA).

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text: The global Moran’s I says the map is clustered. Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA), here local Moran’s I, say where: they give each area its own statistic, test and cluster type.

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
One statistic per area

loc <- localmoran(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
head(round(loc, 3))

      Ii   E.Ii Var.Ii   Z.Ii Pr(z != E(Ii))
1 -0.228 -0.001  0.016 -1.773          0.076
2  0.094 -0.007  0.132  0.277          0.781
3 -0.043 -0.052  1.923  0.006          0.995
4  0.403 -0.007  0.140  1.099          0.272
5  0.018 -0.002  0.045  0.095          0.924
6  0.327 -0.004  0.060  1.346          0.178









Column
Meaning




Ii
local Moran’s I of this area (positive: similar to its neighbours; negative: unlike them)


E.Ii, Var.Ii
its expectation and variance with no pattern


Z.Ii
z-score


Pr(z != E(Ii))
two-sided p-value



The sum of the local values divided by the sum of the weights equals the global I: the global statistic is the average of the local ones.

c(global = unname(moran.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1]),
  mean_local = mean(loc[, "Ii"])) |> round(3)

    global mean_local 
     0.499      0.499

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
Cluster types from the quadrants
Combine the quadrant from the Moran scatterplot with significance:

z <- as.numeric(scale(blocks$dengue_per_100k)); lag_z <- lag.listw(lw, z, zero.policy = TRUE)
p <- loc[, "Pr(z != E(Ii))"]
blocks$lisa <- case_when(
  p >= 0.05 ~ "Not significant",
  z > 0 & lag_z > 0 ~ "High-High (hot spot)",
  z < 0 & lag_z < 0 ~ "Low-Low (cold spot)",
  z > 0 & lag_z < 0 ~ "High-Low (outlier)",
  TRUE ~ "Low-High (outlier)")
blocks$lisa <- factor(blocks$lisa, levels = c("High-High (hot spot)", "Low-Low (cold spot)", "High-Low (outlier)", "Low-High (outlier)", "Not significant"))
table(blocks$lisa)


High-High (hot spot)  Low-Low (cold spot)   High-Low (outlier) 
                  11                   10                    1 
  Low-High (outlier)      Not significant 
                   0                   57 



cols <- c("High-High (hot spot)" = "#d7191c", "Low-Low (cold spot)" = "#2c7bb6", "High-Low (outlier)" = "#fdae61", "Low-High (outlier)" = "#abd9e9", "Not significant" = "grey90")
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = lisa), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) + scale_fill_manual(values = cols, drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "LISA cluster map of dengue incidence", subtitle = "p < 0.05, unadjusted, queen weights") + theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))








In this synthetic district the generator planted a hot spot in the south-east, a cold spot in the north-west and one high block inside the cold area. The map should show all three: the red group, the blue group, and an orange High-Low outlier.

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
Multiple testing
You just ran 79 tests. At 5% about 4 areas appear “significant” by chance alone, and the tests are correlated because neighbouring areas share neighbours. Adjust the p-values with p.adjust() or be cautious:

p_fdr <- p.adjust(p, method = "fdr")                 # adjust the 79 p-values (Benjamini-Hochberg)
c(unadjusted_p_lt_05 = sum(p < 0.05), fdr_adjusted_p_lt_05 = sum(p_fdr < 0.05), bonferroni_p_lt_05 = sum(p.adjust(p, "bonferroni") < 0.05))

  unadjusted_p_lt_05 fdr_adjusted_p_lt_05   bonferroni_p_lt_05 
                  22                   13                    3 



"bonferroni" is the most conservative, "fdr" (Benjamini-Hochberg) controls the false discovery rate and is a sensible default.
Treat LISA as exploratory: it shows where to look, not proof of a cluster in each area.

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
A permutation version
The analytical p-values assume the data are close to normal. Conditional permutation shuffles the neighbours’ values around each area, and works better for skewed rates:

set.seed(3)
loc_perm <- localmoran_perm(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, nsim = 499, zero.policy = TRUE)
head(round(loc_perm, 3), 3)

      Ii   E.Ii Var.Ii   Z.Ii Pr(z != E(Ii)) Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim Pr(folded) Sim
1 -0.228 -0.007  0.017 -1.681          0.093              0.084          0.042
2  0.094 -0.028  0.130  0.338          0.735              0.752          0.376
3 -0.043  0.001  2.039 -0.031          0.976              0.980          0.492
  Skewness Kurtosis
1    0.151   -0.003
2   -0.188   -0.010
3    0.186   -0.158

c(analytic_sig = sum(p < 0.05), permutation_sig = sum(loc_perm[, "Pr(z != E(Ii))"] < 0.05))

   analytic_sig permutation_sig 
             22              22

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
Reading cluster maps

A High-High area has a high value and high-value neighbours: a hot spot, where to look for a shared cause or to target an intervention.
A High-Low area is a spatial outlier: unusually high among low neighbours (a local outbreak, a data problem, a special site). Check the record before interpreting.
The result depends on the weights, the variable (rates, not counts) and the significance rule. Say which you used.
Each area’s cluster status uses its neighbours, so a hot spot typically covers several areas, not one.

title: Local Moran’s I (LISA)
text:
Take-home

Local Moran’s I gives a statistic and p-value per area; the quadrant tells the cluster type (HH, LL, HL, LH).
You ran many tests: adjust ("fdr") or treat the result as exploratory, and consider permutation p-values.
Pair the global test with the local map, and always report variable, weights and adjustment.
Next: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, join counts and the scan statistic.

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Note



This module builds on Quarto Basics. It assumes you can create and render a .qmd file and write basic code chunks.

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
What you will learn

Parameterised reports — run the same document for different subgroups
Inline R code — embed values directly in prose
Cross-references for figures and tables
Multiple output formats from one source file
Integrating gtsummary tables in Quarto

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Parameterised Reports
Parameters let you run the same document with different inputs — for example, generating one report per hospital, intervention group, or region.

1. Declare parameters in the YAML header
---
title: "Site Report"
params:
  site_name: "Site A"
  intervention: "Control"
---


2. Use parameters in code

# params$site_name and params$intervention are available as R objects
site_data <- overall_up |>
  filter(site == params$site_name,
         intervention == params$intervention)

nrow(site_data)



3. Render with different parameter values

# Render from R for a specific site
quarto::quarto_render(
  input  = "site_report.qmd",
  output_file = "site_a_report.html",
  execute_params = list(
    site_name    = "Site A",
    intervention = "Intervention"
  )
)



4. Batch render — one file per site

library(purrr)

sites <- c("Site A", "Site B", "Site C")

walk(sites, \(site) {
  quarto::quarto_render(
    input          = "site_report.qmd",
    output_file    = paste0(tolower(gsub(" ", "_", site)), "_report.html"),
    execute_params = list(site_name = site)
  )
})

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Inline R Code
Embedding computed values directly in text avoids copy-paste errors and keeps your document reproducible.
Syntax:
200

# In a code chunk (runs silently):
n_total  <- nrow(overall_up)
mean_age <- round(mean(overall_up$current_age, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

In Quarto prose:
The study enrolled 200 participants with a mean age of
NA years (SD = 14.3).
Rendered output:

The study enrolled 1 248 participants with a mean age of 38.4 years (SD = 11.2).







Tip



Compute all summary values in one early code chunk marked #| include: false, then reference them via inline code throughout the document.

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Cross-References
Cross-references auto-number figures and tables and create clickable links.

Figures
Add a label that starts with fig- and a fig-cap:
```{r}
#| label: fig-sbp-hist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of baseline systolic blood pressure."
ggplot(overall_up, aes(x = sbp_0m)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Systolic BP (mmHg)", y = "Count")
```
Reference in text: @fig-sbp-hist → renders as “Figure 1”


Tables
Add a label starting with tbl- and a tbl-cap:
```{r}
#| label: tbl-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Baseline characteristics of study participants."
library(gtsummary)
overall_up |>
  select(current_age, sex, tobacco_type, fuel_type) |>
  tbl_summary()
```
Reference in text: @tbl-demographics → renders as “Table 1”

title: Quarto — Dynamic Documents
text:
Multiple Output Formats
One .qmd file can produce HTML, PDF, and Word output.
---
title: "Study Report"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    theme: flatly
  pdf:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
  docx:
    toc: true
---
Render all formats at once:
quarto render study_report.qmd






WarningPDF requirements



PDF rendering requires a LaTeX installation. Install tinytex from R:
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()

Quarto — Dynamic Documents

Option
Effect




echo: false
Hide code, show output


include: false
Run code silently (no output shown)


eval: false
Show code but don’t run it

Suppress warnings

Suppress package messages


fig-width: 8
Figure width in inches

Figure height in inches


fig-dpi: 300
Resolution for saved figures



Set globally in YAML to apply to all chunks:
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggstatsplot is an R package that combines statistical tests and publication-ready visualisations in a single function call. Each plot automatically selects, runs, and annotates the appropriate statistical test based on your data, displaying results directly on the figure.
This removes a common workflow bottleneck: running a test in one place, building a plot in another, and manually annotating results.

install.packages("ggstatsplot")
library(ggstatsplot)

Why use it?

One function produces both the visual and the statistical result
Automatically annotates effect sizes and confidence intervals
Sensible defaults — works out of the box for most common comparisons
Output is a ggplot2 object, so you can add layers or themes as usual

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
section: Core functions covered in this module
text:
Core functions covered in this module



Function
Use case




ggbetweenstats()
Compare groups (independent samples)


ggscatterstats()
Correlation between two continuous variables


gghistostats()
Distribution of a single continuous variable

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggbetweenstats() — Group Comparisons
Use this when you want to compare a continuous variable across two or more independent groups.

library(ggstatsplot)

# Compare systolic BP across fuel type groups
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,         # grouping variable (categorical)
  y     = sbp_0m,            # outcome variable (continuous)
  title = "Systolic BP by Fuel Type"
)

What the output shows:

A violin + boxplot combination with individual data points
The statistical test used (Welch’s ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis, chosen automatically)
The p-value, effect size (η² or ε²), and confidence interval
Pairwise comparisons (if more than 2 groups)

Choosing parametric vs non-parametric:

# Force non-parametric (Kruskal-Wallis)
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  type  = "nonparametric"   # "parametric", "nonparametric", "robust", "bayes"
)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggscatterstats() — Correlation
Use this when you want to examine the relationship between two continuous variables.

ggscatterstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = current_age,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  title = "Age vs Systolic BP at Baseline"
)

What the output shows:

A scatter plot with a linear trend line and confidence band
Pearson (or Spearman) correlation coefficient, r
p-value and 95% confidence interval for r
Marginal histograms on both axes

Using Spearman instead of Pearson:

ggscatterstats(
  data = overall_up,
  x    = current_age,
  y    = sbp_0m,
  type = "nonparametric"   # uses Spearman's rho
)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
gghistostats() — Distribution
Use this when you want to visualise the distribution of a single continuous variable with a one-sample test.

gghistostats(
  data     = overall_up,
  x        = current_age,
  title    = "Distribution of Age at Enrolment",
  test.value = 40          # hypothesised population mean
)

What the output shows:

Histogram with overlaid density curve
One-sample t-test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank) against the specified test.value
Mean, median, and their confidence intervals

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
Reading the statistical annotation
Every ggstatsplot figure includes a subtitle with the test results in a standardised format:
Welch's ANOVA, F(2, 147.3) = 5.23, p = 0.006, ω² = 0.06, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14]



Component
Meaning




Test name
Which test was used (selected automatically)


Test statistic
F, t, χ², H etc.


p-value
Statistical significance


Effect size
Practical significance (ω², d, r, etc.)


95% CI
Uncertainty around the effect size









TipInterpreting effect sizes




η² / ω²: Small ≈ 0.01, Medium ≈ 0.06, Large ≈ 0.14 (for ANOVA)
Cohen’s d: Small ≈ 0.2, Medium ≈ 0.5, Large ≈ 0.8 (for t-tests)
r: Small ≈ 0.1, Medium ≈ 0.3, Large ≈ 0.5 (for correlation)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
Quick reference

# Two-group comparison
ggbetweenstats(data = df, x = group, y = outcome)

# Correlation
ggscatterstats(data = df, x = var1, y = var2)

# Distribution
gghistostats(data = df, x = continuous_var, test.value = 0)

title: Plotting Tools
text:
This chapter introduces various tools and libraries available in R for creating visualizations. It covers base R plotting functions, as well as popular packages like ggplot2 and lattice, which offer advanced capabilities for creating complex and customizable plots.


R’s built-in plotting functions provide a solid foundation for data visualization:


# Scatter plot
plot(x = mtcars$wt, y = mtcars$mpg,
     xlab = "Weight", ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Scatter Plot Example")

# Line plot
plot(x = 1:10, y = (1:10)^2, type = "l",
     xlab = "X", ylab = "Y^2")

# Bar plot
barplot(height = c(10, 15, 8, 12),
        names.arg = c("A", "B", "C", "D"))

# Histogram
hist(mtcars$mpg, breaks = 10,
     xlab = "Miles per Gallon",
     main = "Histogram of MPG")



# Multiple plots in one window
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))  # 2x2 grid

plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
hist(mtcars$mpg)
boxplot(mtcars$mpg ~ mtcars$cyl)
plot(density(mtcars$mpg))

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))  # Reset to single plot




ggplot2 is the most popular R package for data visualization, based on the Grammar of Graphics:


library(ggplot2)

# Basic scatter plot
ggplot(data = mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Adding aesthetics
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "MPG vs Weight by Cylinders",
       x = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
       y = "Miles per Gallon")



# Points, lines, bars
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))

p + geom_point()           # Scatter plot
p + geom_smooth()          # Smooth line
p + geom_line()            # Line plot
p + geom_bar(stat = "identity")  # Bar plot
p + geom_histogram()       # Histogram
p + geom_boxplot()         # Box plot



# Faceting
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ cyl) +
  theme_minimal()

# Custom themes
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  ggtitle("Custom Theme Example")




Lattice provides trellis graphics for multivariate data:
library(lattice)

# Scatter plot matrix
splom(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])

# Conditional plots
xyplot(mpg ~ wt | factor(cyl), data = mtcars,
       layout = c(3, 1))

# 3D plots
cloud(mpg ~ wt * hp, data = mtcars)





library(plotly)

# Convert ggplot to interactive
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
ggplotly(p)

# Native plotly
plot_ly(mtcars, x = ~wt, y = ~mpg, type = "scatter", mode = "markers")



library(ggvis)

# Interactive ggplot2-like syntax
mtcars %>%
  ggvis(x = ~wt, y = ~mpg) %>%
  layer_points() %>%
  add_tooltip(function(df) paste("Weight:", df$wt, "MPG:", df$mpg))






library(ggstatsplot)

# Statistical plots with tests
ggbetweenstats(data = mtcars, x = cyl, y = mpg)



library(ggplot2)
library(maps)

# Basic map
world <- map_data("world")
ggplot(world, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "lightblue", color = "black")



library(igraph)
library(ggraph)

# Create network
g <- make_ring(10)
ggraph(g, layout = "circle") +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point(size = 5)





Base R: Quick plots, statistical graphics
ggplot2: Publication-quality static plots, complex customizations
Lattice: Multivariate data, trellis displays
plotly/ggvis: Interactive web-based visualizations
Specialized packages: Domain-specific visualizations (maps, networks, etc.)





Know your data: Choose plot types that best represent your data
Keep it simple: Avoid clutter, focus on the message
Use color effectively: Consider colorblind-friendly palettes
Label clearly: Include informative titles, axis labels, legends
Test different tools: Experiment with different packages for the best result

title: Debugging Plots
text:
Debugging plots are essential tools for diagnosing issues in data visualization and analysis. They help identify problems such as incorrect data representation, scaling issues, or unexpected patterns in the data. In this guide, we will explore various techniques and tools for creating effective debugging plots.





Missing or incorrect data types
# Check data types
str(mtcars)

# Check for missing values
sum(is.na(mtcars))

# Visualize missing patterns
library(naniar)
vis_miss(mtcars)
Outliers affecting scales
# Check for outliers
boxplot(mtcars$mpg)

# Use robust statistics
library(robustbase)
summary(mtcars$mpg)





Mapping vs Setting Aesthetics
# Correct: Map color to variable
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point()

# Incorrect: Setting color globally
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "red")  # This sets all points to red
Factor Level Issues
# Check factor levels
levels(mtcars$cyl)

# Reorder factors if needed
mtcars$cyl <- factor(mtcars$cyl, levels = c("4", "6", "8"))
Geom Conflicts
# Error: Can't use geom_bar with y aesthetic
# ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) + geom_bar()

# Correct: Use stat = "identity"
ggplot(data, aes(x = category, y = value)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity")







# Check ggplot object structure
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
str(p)

# View plot data
p$data
p$mapping



# Build plot incrementally
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg))
print(p1)  # Should show empty plot

p2 <- p1 + geom_point()
print(p2)  # Check if points appear

p3 <- p2 + theme_minimal()
print(p3)  # Check theme application



# Enable ggplot2 debugging
options(ggplot2.debug = TRUE)

# Check for warnings
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()






# Problem: Length mismatch
# ggplot(data, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var, color = short_vector))

# Solution: Ensure vectors are same length or use single values
ggplot(data, aes(x = x_var, y = y_var, color = factor(category)))



# Problem: Wrong scale type
# ggplot(data, aes(x = factor_var, y = numeric_var)) + scale_x_continuous()

# Solution: Use appropriate scale
ggplot(data, aes(x = factor_var, y = numeric_var)) + scale_x_discrete()



# Problem: Typo in parameter name
# geom_point(size = 3)  # Correct
# geom_point(siz = 3)   # Incorrect

# Solution: Check documentation
?geom_point






# Residual plots for model diagnostics
model <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
plot(model)

# QQ plots for normality
qqnorm(mtcars$mpg)
qqline(mtcars$mpg)



# Correlation plots
library(corrplot)
corrplot(cor(mtcars))

# Pairs plots
pairs(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "hp")])



# Plot data distributions
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = mpg)) + 
  geom_histogram() + 
  facet_wrap(~ cyl)

# Check for data issues
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = rownames(mtcars)), check_overlap = TRUE)






# When plot fails
tryCatch({
  ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
}, error = function(e) {
  print(e)
  traceback()
})



library(profvis)

# Profile plotting code
profvis({
  p <- ggplot(large_dataset, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_point()
  print(p)
})



# Check memory usage
gc()

# For large datasets, use sampling
sample_data <- mtcars[sample(nrow(mtcars), 1000, replace = TRUE), ]
ggplot(sample_data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()





Start simple: Build plots incrementally
Check data first: Validate input data before plotting
Use reproducible examples: Create minimal examples that reproduce issues
Read error messages carefully: They often point to the exact problem
Check package versions: Ensure compatible versions of ggplot2 and extensions
Use debugging tools: Leverage R’s debugging functions and ggplot2’s debug options
Document fixes: Keep notes on solutions for future reference

title: Statistical Tests and Analysis
text:
This section covers common statistical tests used in medical research, implemented in R.



# Load necessary libraries
library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(gtsummary)

# Example data
data <- data.frame(
  age = rnorm(100, 50, 10),
  blood_pressure = rnorm(100, 120, 15),
  treatment = sample(c("A", "B"), 100, replace = TRUE)
)

# Summary statistics
data %>% 
  tbl_summary()











Characteristic
N = 1001




age
50 (43, 56)


blood_pressure
122 (114, 132)


treatment




    A
58 (58%)


    B
42 (42%)



1 Median (Q1, Q3); n (%)














# Two-sample t-test
t.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
t = -0.79303, df = 77.882, p-value = 0.4302
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -9.099004  3.915096
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       121.0755        123.6674 






# Create categorical data
data$outcome <- sample(c("Improved", "Not Improved"), 100, replace = TRUE)

# Chi-square test
chisq.test(table(data$treatment, data$outcome))


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  table(data$treatment, data$outcome)
X-squared = 0.1916, df = 1, p-value = 0.6616













Outcome
Groups / predictor
Usual test




Continuous
2 independent groups
Two-sample (Welch) t-test


Continuous
same people measured twice (before/after)
Paired t-test


Continuous, skewed or small sample
2 independent groups
Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney)


Continuous
3 or more groups
One-way ANOVA (Kruskal-Wallis if skewed)


Categorical (yes/no)
categorical
Chi-square test (Fisher’s exact if expected counts are small)







t.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
t = -0.79303, df = 77.882, p-value = 0.4302
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -9.099004  3.915096
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       121.0755        123.6674 



R uses Welch’s t-test by default (does not assume equal variances).
The confidence interval is for the first group minus the second (A − B), so the sign follows the order of the groups.
The sample estimates show each group’s mean.





# paired: the same 30 people before and after
before <- rnorm(30, 140, 12)
after  <- before - rnorm(30, 5, 6)
t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  before and after
t = 4.5517, df = 29, p-value = 8.8e-05
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.745638 7.226368
sample estimates:
mean difference 
       4.986003 

# non-parametric alternative for two independent groups
wilcox.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
W = 1069, p-value = 0.2997
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0






A p-value says how surprising the data would be if there were no true difference.
It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and not the probability the result is “due to chance”.
It says nothing about the size or importance of the difference: look at the estimate and its confidence interval.
A large p-value is weak evidence against “no difference”. It is not proof that there is none.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Importance of Data Analysis


Making Sense of Data

Driving Informed Decisions — strategic choices based on evidence, not intuition
Identifying Patterns and Insights — uncovering hidden relationships in data
Optimizing Processes — streamline operations using performance metrics
Supporting Innovation — fuel new ideas and solutions


Research Perspective

Evidence-Based Research — validate hypotheses and draw reliable conclusions
Mitigating Risk — identify potential errors before they reach conclusions
Improving Reproducibility — ensures findings can be replicated
Ethical Responsibility — especially critical in clinical and health research

title: Data Analysis
text:
Why Test Selection Matters
Choosing the wrong test leads to Type I (false positive) or Type II (false negative) errors.







Reason
Detail




Accuracy & Validity
Test must match data nature and research question


Avoiding Errors
Wrong test → misleading conclusions


Reproducibility
Correct test ensures others can replicate findings


Meeting Objectives
Test must align with the hypothesis


Ethical Responsibility
In clinical research, conclusions affect real policy

title: Data Analysis
text:
Decision Framework — Overview

The choice of statistical test depends on: variable type → number of groups → normality → independence of observations







Note


Flowchart placeholder
Insert here: Overall test selection flowchart — starting from variable type (Categorical vs Continuous), then branching by number of groups, then normality, then paired vs unpaired.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Types of Variables






Note


Flowchart placeholder
Insert here: Variable classification diagram — Qualitative (Nominal, Ordinal) and Quantitative (Discrete, Continuous). Can also show examples relevant to your dataset such as sex, wealth index, age, SBP, FBS.





Categorical / Qualitative

Nominal — no order (e.g., sex, past history of DM)
Ordinal — ordered categories (e.g., wealth index: poorest → richest)
Binary / Dichotomous — two categories (e.g., screened: Yes/No)


Numerical / Quantitative

Discrete — whole numbers (e.g., number of visits)
Continuous — any value in a range (e.g., age, SBP, height, FBS)

title: Data Analysis
text:
Categorical Variables — Frequency Tables
Use table() for base R frequency counts or group_by() + reframe() for tidy output.

# Base R approach
freq_table <- table(p$past_history_of_diabetes)
prop_table <- prop.table(freq_table)

combined_table <- data.frame(
  Frequency = freq_table,
  Percentage = round(prop_table * 100, 2)
)
combined_table

  Frequency.Var1 Frequency.Freq Percentage.Var1 Percentage.Freq
1             no            597              no           94.61
2            yes             34             yes            5.39

# Frequency and percentage using dplyr — unordered factor
summary_table <- p %>%
  mutate(wealth_index = factor(wealth_index_of_participants)) |>
  group_by(wealth_index) %>%
  reframe(

    Percentage = paste(round(n() * 100 / nrow(p), 2), "%")

title: Data Analysis
text:
Why Check Normality?
Many parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA, Pearson’s r) assume normally distributed data.
Failing to check normality can lead to:

Invalid p-values
Wrong test selection
Misleading conclusions

Two approaches: Visual methods + Statistical tests

title: Data Analysis
text:
Visual Methods — Histogram

hist(
  p$age_of_participants,
  main  = "Histogram with Density Line",
  xlab  = "Age",
  ylab  = "Density",
  col   = "grey",
  border = "black",
  freq  = FALSE
)
lines(density(p$age_of_participants), col = "red", lwd = 2)


A roughly bell-shaped curve suggests normality. Skewed or multimodal histograms indicate non-normality.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Visual Methods — QQ Plot

qqnorm(p$sbp_in_mm_hg, main = "Q-Q Plot: SBP")
qqline(p$sbp_in_mm_hg, col = "red")


Points should follow the red diagonal line closely if the data are normally distributed. Deviations at the tails indicate non-normality.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Statistical Tests — Shapiro-Wilk
Best for small samples (n ≤ 50). Randomly sample if n > 50.

p1 <- p[sample(nrow(p), 50), ]
s_test <- shapiro.test(p1$age_of_participants)
s_test


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  p1$age_of_participants
W = 0.95857, p-value = 0.07744



Interpretation: p > 0.05 → data does not significantly deviate from normality (cannot reject H₀ of normality).

title: Data Analysis
text:
Statistical Tests — Kolmogorov-Smirnov
Suitable for larger samples. Compares distribution to a theoretical normal.

ks_test <- ks.test(p$sbp_in_mm_hg, "pnorm",
                   mean = mean(p$sbp_in_mm_hg),
                   sd   = sd(p$sbp_in_mm_hg))
ks_test


    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  p$sbp_in_mm_hg
D = 0.052082, p-value = 0.06522
alternative hypothesis: two-sided



Note: Use options(scipen = 999) to display p-values in decimal format instead of scientific notation.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Statistical Tests — Anderson-Darling
More sensitive to tails than KS test. Requires nortest package.

ad_test <- ad.test(p$height)
ad_test

A = 0.27928, p-value = 0.6458

Package

title: Data Analysis
text:
Decision Framework — Categorical






Note


Flowchart placeholder
Insert here: Categorical variable test selection flowchart — branching from number of groups (1, 2, >2) and paired vs unpaired, leading to: Chi-square goodness of fit → Chi-square test of independence / Fisher’s exact → McNemar / Exact McNemar → Chi-square m×n / Monte Carlo.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit — 1 Group
Tests whether the observed distribution matches an expected distribution.

observed <- table(p$ever_screened_for_bp)
total    <- sum(observed)
expected <- c(1/2, 1/2) * total

chisq_test <- chisq.test(x = observed, p = expected / sum(expected))
chisq_test


    Chi-squared test for given probabilities

data:  observed
X-squared = 80.23, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16



Assumption: Expected frequency ≥ 5 in each cell.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square Test — 2 Binary Groups (Expected ≥ 5)
Tests association between two categorical variables using a contingency table.

table_gender_dm <- table(p$sex_of_participants, p$past_history_of_diabetes)
table_gender_dm

        
          no yes
  female 332  17
  male   265  17

chisq_m5 <- chisq.test(table_gender_dm, correct = FALSE)
chisq_m5


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  table_gender_dm
X-squared = 0.40978, df = 1, p-value = 0.5221

# Check expected frequencies
chisq_m5$expected

        
               no      yes
  female 330.1949 18.80507
  male   266.8051 15.19493



Use correct = FALSE to apply the standard Pearson Chi-square (no Yates correction).

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square — Yates Continuity Correction
Yates correction subtracts 0.5 from the absolute difference between observed and expected frequency before squaring.

# With Yates correction (correct = TRUE is default for 2x2 tables)
chisq.test(table_gender_dm, correct = TRUE)


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  table_gender_dm
X-squared = 0.2142, df = 1, p-value = 0.6435



Apply when sample sizes are small or expected frequencies approach 5.

title: Data Analysis
text:
When Expected Frequency < 5
Two options: Monte Carlo simulation or Fisher’s Exact Test.

table_htn_dm <- table(p$ever_screened_for_bp, p$past_history_of_diabetes)

# Monte Carlo simulation (B = number of replicates, min p = 1/(B+1))
chisq_mc <- chisq.test(table_htn_dm, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
chisq_mc


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with simulated p-value (based on 2000
    replicates)

data:  table_htn_dm
X-squared = 11.381, df = NA, p-value = 0.002999

# Fisher's Exact Test
fisher_test <- fisher.test(table_htn_dm)
fisher_test


    Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data

data:  table_htn_dm
p-value = 0.0002606
alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
  2.032418 70.633884
sample estimates:
odds ratio 
  8.105124

title: Data Analysis
text:
Chi-Square — m × n Contingency Table
Use when both variables have more than two categories.

table_mar_wealth <- table(
  p$marital_status_of_participants,
  p$wealth_index_of_participants
)
table_mar_wealth

                       
                        middle poorer poorest richer richest
  currently married         82     68      17    119     115
  formerly/ever married     31     16      13     22      14
  never married             34     22       4     36      38

chisq_mn <- chisq.test(table_mar_wealth)
chisq_mn


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  table_mar_wealth
X-squared = 26.65, df = 8, p-value = 0.0008122

# Monte Carlo if expected frequencies < 5
chisq_mn_mc <- chisq.test(table_mar_wealth, simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 2000)
chisq_mn_mc


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with simulated p-value (based on 2000
    replicates)

data:  table_mar_wealth
X-squared = 26.65, df = NA, p-value = 0.002499

title: Data Analysis
text:
McNemar Test — Paired Binary Responses
Use when the same participants are measured twice on a binary outcome (e.g., before and after treatment).

table_bfr_aftr <- table(p$pain_foot_bfr, p$pain_foot_aftr)
table_bfr_aftr

     
       No Yes
  No  176 159
  Yes 150 146

mcnemar_test <- mcnemar.test(table_bfr_aftr)
mcnemar_test


    McNemar's Chi-squared test with continuity correction

data:  table_bfr_aftr
McNemar's chi-squared = 0.20712, df = 1, p-value = 0.649



Assumption: Discordant cells (b + c) should be ≥ 25. If < 25, use exact McNemar.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Exact McNemar Test

exact_mcnemar <- exact2x2::mcnemar.exact(table_bfr_aftr)
exact_mcnemar


    Exact McNemar test (with central confidence intervals)

data:  table_bfr_aftr
b = 159, c = 150, p-value = 0.6491
alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.8426767 1.3339030
sample estimates:
odds ratio 
      1.06 





Situation
Test

McNemar

title: Data Analysis
text:
Decision Framework — Continuous






Note


Flowchart placeholder
Insert here: Continuous variable test selection flowchart — branching from number of groups (1, 2, >2), then normality (normal vs non-normal), then paired vs unpaired, leading to: Z-test / One-sample t → Independent t / Paired t / Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon Matched Pairs → One-way ANOVA / Repeated Measures ANOVA / Kruskal-Wallis / Friedman.

title: Data Analysis
text:
One Group — Z Test
Use when population SD is known and n > 30.

pr  <- p |> filter(wealth_index_of_participants == "richer")
mu  <- mean(p$age_of_participants)
sigma <- sd(p$age_of_participants)

s_mean <- mean(pr$age_of_participants)
n      <- length(pr$age_of_participants)
z      <- (s_mean - mu) / (sigma / sqrt(n))

p_two_tailed     <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z)))
p_one_tailed_gt  <- 1 - pnorm(z)
p_one_tailed_lt  <- pnorm(z)

cat("Z =", round(z, 3),
    "\nTwo-tailed p =", round(p_two_tailed, 4),
    "\nOne-tailed (greater) p =", round(p_one_tailed_gt, 4))

Z = -0.879 
Two-tailed p = 0.3794 
One-tailed (greater) p = 0.8103

title: Data Analysis
text:
One Group — One-Sample t Test
Use when population SD is unknown or n < 30.

pp <- p |> filter(wealth_index_of_participants == "poorest")

t_test <- t.test(pp$age_of_participants, mu = mu)
t_test


    One Sample t-test

data:  pp$age_of_participants
t = 1.5716, df = 33, p-value = 0.1256
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 43.84786
95 percent confidence interval:
 42.28702 56.00709
sample estimates:
mean of x 
 49.14706 





Test
Population SD
n




One-sample Z
Known
> 30


One-sample t
Unknown
Any; especially < 30

title: Data Analysis
text:
Two Groups — Testing Equal Variance
Before an independent t-test, verify the equal variance assumption.

# Levene's test (robust to non-normality)
car::leveneTest(weight ~ sex_of_participants, data = p)

Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = median)
       Df F value Pr(>F)
group   1  0.0453 0.8316
      629               

# Bartlett's test (assumes normality)
bartlett.test(weight ~ sex_of_participants, data = p)


    Bartlett test of homogeneity of variances

data:  weight by sex_of_participants
Bartlett's K-squared = 0.21685, df = 1, p-value = 0.6415



Interpretation: p < 0.05 → variances are NOT equal → use var.equal = FALSE in t.test.

title: Data Analysis
section: Two Groups — Independent t Test (Unpaired, Normal)
text:
Two Groups — Independent t Test (Unpaired, Normal)

ind_t_test <- t.test(weight ~ sex_of_participants,
                     var.equal = TRUE,
                     data = p)
ind_t_test


    Two Sample t-test

data:  weight by sex_of_participants
t = 0.61333, df = 629, p-value = 0.5399
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group female and group male is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -1.662463  3.172588
sample estimates:
mean in group female   mean in group male 
            70.04272             69.28766 








Note


Flowchart placeholder
Insert here: Equal variance flowchart — Levene/Bartlett test → p < 0.05 (unequal variances, Welch t-test) vs p ≥ 0.05 (equal variances, standard independent t-test).

title: Data Analysis
text:
Two Groups — Paired t Test (Normal)
Use when the same participants are measured at two time points.

paired_t_test <- t.test(p$fbs_presentation, p$fbs_6_months, paired = TRUE)
paired_t_test


    Paired t-test

data:  p$fbs_presentation and p$fbs_6_months
t = 26.186, df = 630, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 14.06450 16.34501
sample estimates:
mean difference 
       15.20475 



Assumption: Differences between paired observations must be normally distributed.

title: Data Analysis
text:
Two Groups — Mann-Whitney U (Non-Normal, Unpaired)
Non-parametric alternative to the independent t-test. Based on ranks, not raw values.

mann_whit <- wilcox.test(sbp_presentation ~ sex_of_participants,
                         data = p,
                         correct = FALSE)
mann_whit


    Wilcoxon rank sum test

data:  sbp_presentation by sex_of_participants
W = 51423, p-value = 0.3308
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0



Use correct = TRUE (continuity correction) when: sample size < 100, or data is ordinal/discrete.

title: Data Analysis
section: Two Groups — Wilcoxon Matched Pairs (Non-Normal, Paired)
text:
Two Groups — Wilcoxon Matched Pairs (Non-Normal, Paired)
Non-parametric alternative to the paired t-test.

wilcox_paired <- wilcox.test(p$sbp_presentation, p$sbp_6_months, paired = TRUE)
wilcox_paired


    Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

data:  p$sbp_presentation and p$sbp_6_months
V = 157262, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0



Assumption: Differences between paired values should be symmetrically distributed (not necessarily normal).
