title: Practical Application
text:
Publication Figure - Code


Code
# Treatment effect with confidence intervals
model <- lm(SysBP_12m ~ TreatmentGroup + Age + BMI_0m + SysBP_0m,
           data = health_data)

library(ggeffects)
effects <- ggpredict(model, terms = "TreatmentGroup")

p <- plot(effects) +
  labs(title = "Treatment Effect on Systolic Blood Pressure",
       subtitle = "Adjusted for age, BMI, and baseline BP",
       x = "Treatment Group",
       y = "Predicted Systolic BP (mmHg)",
       caption = "Error bars: 95% confidence intervals. n=500 per group.") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  )

# Save high-res
ggsave("figure1.tiff", p, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)
ggsave("figure1.eps", p, width = 7, height = 5, device = cairo_ps)

title: Regression Analysis
text: Regression models describe and quantify the relationship between an outcome and one or more predictors. This module builds up in tiers — start with a single predictor, then add predictors, then move on to diagnostics and logistic regression.

title: Regression Analysis
text:
Regression Diagnostics
A fitted model is only trustworthy once its assumptions have been checked.

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(model)









# Residuals vs fitted, and a normal Q-Q check
qqnorm(residuals(model))
qqline(residuals(model), col = "red")








Watch for: non-random patterns in residuals-vs-fitted (non-linearity), points far off the Q-Q line (non-normal residuals), and high-leverage points in the residuals-vs-leverage panel.

title: Regression Analysis
text:
Cox Proportional Hazards Regression
For time-to-event outcomes (e.g. time to recovery, time to relapse), use survival::coxph() instead of lm()/glm(). It models the hazard of the event happening at any given time, adjusted for covariates.

library(survival)

data$time  <- rexp(100, rate = 0.05)
data$event <- rbinom(100, 1, 0.7)   # 1 = event observed, 0 = censored

cox_model <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ age + treatment, data = data)
summary(cox_model)

title: Regression Analysis
text:
Model Diagnostics with performance
The performance package gives a quick, standardized diagnostic check for a fitted model, going further than the base-R diagnostic plots used earlier.

library(performance)

check_model(model)









r2(model)

# R2 for Linear Regression
       R2: 0.000
  adj. R2: -0.020

check_collinearity(model)

# Check for Multicollinearity

Low Correlation

      Term  VIF  VIF 95% CI adj. VIF Tolerance Tolerance 95% CI
       age 1.00 [1.00, Inf]     1.00      1.00     [0.00, 1.00]
 treatment 1.00 [1.00, Inf]     1.00      1.00     [0.00, 1.00]


check_model() bundles several checks — linearity, homogeneity of variance, normality of residuals, influential observations, and collinearity — into one panel. check_collinearity() reports Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) on their own; values above roughly 5 suggest predictors are too correlated with each other to interpret their individual coefficients reliably.

title: Advanced Exporting Techniques
text:
This chapter covers advanced techniques for exporting plots, including programmatic generation, batch processing, custom devices, and integration with other tools.




library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

# Create plots for each cylinder group
plots <- mtcars %>%
  split(.$cyl) %>%
  map(~ ggplot(.x, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + 
        geom_point() + 
        ggtitle(paste("Cylinders:", .x$cyl[1])))

# Save each plot
walk2(plots, names(plots), 
      ~ ggsave(filename = paste0("plot_cyl_", .x, ".png"), 
               plot = .y, 
               width = 6, height = 4))



# Generate timestamped filenames
timestamp <- format(Sys.time(), "%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")

ggsave(paste0("analysis_plot_", timestamp, ".pdf"), 
       plot = p, 
       width = 8, height = 6)






save_plot_multiple_formats <- function(plot, filename_base, 
                                     formats = c("png", "pdf", "svg")) {
  for (fmt in formats) {
    filename <- paste0(filename_base, ".", fmt)
    ggsave(filename, plot, width = 8, height = 6)
  }
}

# Usage
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
save_plot_multiple_formats(p, "mtcars_scatter")



datasets <- list(
  mtcars = mtcars,
  iris = iris,
  airquality = airquality
)

for (name in names(datasets)) {
  data <- datasets[[name]]
  # Create appropriate plot based on data
  if (name == "mtcars") {
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point()
  } else if (name == "iris") {
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, color = Species)) + 
      geom_point()
  }
  
  ggsave(paste0(name, "_plot.png"), p, width = 6, height = 4)
}






library(Cairo)

# High-quality PNG
CairoPNG("high_quality.png", width = 800, height = 600, 
         bg = "white", pointsize = 12)
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
dev.off()

# PDF with embedded fonts
CairoPDF("embedded_fonts.pdf", width = 8, height = 6, 
         family = "Arial")
plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg)
dev.off()

save_high_res <- function(filename, plot_func, ...) {
  png(filename, width = 1200, height = 800, res = 150, ...)
  plot_func()
  dev.off()
}

# Usage
my_plot <- function() {
  plot(mtcars$wt, mtcars$mpg, 
       xlab = "Weight", ylab = "MPG",
       main = "High Resolution Plot")
}

save_high_res("high_res_plot.png", my_plot)

# For large datasets, use sampling or aggregation
large_data <- data.frame(x = rnorm(100000), y = rnorm(100000))

# Option 1: Sample data

check_plot_quality <- function(filename) {
  # Check file exists
  if (!file.exists(filename)) {
    stop("File was not created")
  }
  
  # Check file size (basic quality indicator)
  size <- file.info(filename)$size
  if (size < 1000) {
    warning("File seems too small, may indicate error")
  }
  
  # For images, could check dimensions
  if (grepl("\\.png$", filename)) {
    img <- png::readPNG(filename)
    message("Image dimensions: ", dim(img)[1], "x", dim(img)[2])
  }
}

# Usage
ggsave("test_plot.png", ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) + geom_point())

title: Exporting plots
text: Exporting plots from R can be done in several ways, depending on the desired output format and quality. Here are some common methods to export plots:

title: Exporting plots
text:
Using R’s Built-in Functions
R provides several built-in functions for exporting plots to different formats:

Raster Formats

png(), jpeg(), tiff(), bmp(): These functions save plots in raster formats. You can specify filename, dimensions, and resolution.

# PNG format (good for web)
png("plot.png", width = 800, height = 600, res = 100)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

# High-resolution TIFF for publications
tiff("plot.tiff", width = 8, height = 6, units = "in", res = 300)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()


Vector Formats

pdf(): Saves plots in PDF format, vector-based and scalable.
svg(): Saves plots in SVG format, ideal for web and scalable graphics.

# PDF for high-quality prints
pdf("plot.pdf", width = 8, height = 6)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

# SVG for web use
svg("plot.svg", width = 8, height = 6)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()

title: Exporting plots
text:
Exporting ggplot2 Plots
For ggplot2 plots, the ggsave() function is the most convenient way to export:
library(ggplot2)

# Create a plot
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point()

# Save in different formats
ggsave("plot.png", p, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 150)
ggsave("plot.pdf", p, width = 8, height = 6)
ggsave("plot.svg", p, width = 8, height = 6)

Controlling Output Quality

Resolution (DPI): Higher DPI for print quality (300+), lower for web (72-150)
Dimensions: Specify in inches or pixels
Aspect Ratio: Maintain proportions for consistency

# High-resolution for publications
ggsave("publication_plot.tiff", p, 
       width = 6, height = 4, 
       dpi = 300, 
       device = "tiff")

# Web-optimized PNG
ggsave("web_plot.png", p, 
       width = 800, height = 600, 
       dpi = 100, 
       units = "px")

title: Exporting plots
text:

# Save multiple plots to PDF

print(plot1)
plot2 <- ggplot(data2, aes(x, y)) + geom_line()
print(plot2)
dev.off()


Using Cairo for Better Quality
The Cairo graphics library can provide better quality for some formats:
install.packages("Cairo")
library(Cairo)

CairoPNG("high_quality.png", width = 800, height = 600)
plot(x, y)
dev.off()


Exporting to Clipboard
For quick sharing:
# Windows
savePlot("clipboard", type = "wmf")

# Or for ggplot2
ggsave("clipboard", p, device = "png")

title: Exporting plots
text:
Best Practices

Choose the right format: PDF/SVG for vector graphics, PNG/TIFF for raster
Set appropriate resolution: 300 DPI for print, 72-150 for screen
Consider file size: Vector formats scale better but may be larger
Test outputs: Always check exported files in target applications
Use consistent dimensions: Maintain aspect ratios across exports

title: Exporting plots
text:
Common Issues and Solutions

Plot not saving: Ensure dev.off() is called after plotting
Low quality: Increase DPI or use vector formats
Wrong dimensions: Specify units explicitly (inches, cm, pixels)
Colors not matching: Check color profiles and device settings

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Bayesian Reporting Workflow
The Bayesian approach in ggstatsplot uses the BayesFactor package internally. The goal is to quantify how much evidence exists for or against an effect, rather than simply crossing a significance threshold.

Setting priors

library(ggstatsplot)

# Default Cauchy prior (r = 0.707) — appropriate for most comparisons
ggbetweenstats(
  data         = overall_up,
  x            = intervention,
  y            = sbp_0m,
  type         = "bayes",
  bf.prior     = 0.707,        # scale of Cauchy prior on effect size
  title        = "SBP by Intervention (Bayesian, default prior)"
)

# Narrow prior — use if you expect a small effect
ggbetweenstats(
  data         = overall_up,
  x            = intervention,
  y            = sbp_0m,
  type         = "bayes",
  bf.prior     = 0.5,
  title        = "SBP by Intervention (narrow prior)"
)



Reporting Bayes factors in text
When BF₁₀ = 18.4:

“A Bayesian independent-samples t-test revealed moderate-to-strong evidence for a difference in baseline SBP between intervention groups, BF₁₀ = 18.4, δ = 0.41, 95% credible interval [0.18, 0.65].”

When BF₁₀ = 0.21:

“A Bayesian independent-samples t-test provided moderate evidence in favour of the null hypothesis (no difference in SBP), BF₁₀ = 0.21.”







TipKey distinction: BF₁₀ vs BF₀₁




BF₁₀: evidence for H₁ over H₀ (use when testing for an effect)
BF₀₁ = 1/BF₁₀: evidence for H₀ over H₁ (use when supporting the null)

ggstatsplot reports BF₁₀ by default. To interpret support for H₀, invert it.

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
grouped_* Functions — Faceted Comparisons
The grouped_* variants run the same comparison separately within each level of a grouping variable and combine the results into a faceted plot.

# Compare SBP across tobacco types, separately by sex
grouped_ggbetweenstats(
  data             = overall_up,
  x                = tobacco_type,
  y                = sbp_0m,
  grouping.var     = sex,           # one panel per sex
  title            = "SBP by Tobacco Type, stratified by Sex",
  plotgrid.args    = list(ncol = 2)
)


# Correlation stratified by intervention group
grouped_ggscatterstats(
  data         = overall_up,
  x            = current_age,
  y            = sbp_0m,
  grouping.var = intervention,
  title        = "Age vs SBP by Intervention Group"
)

Available grouped functions:

grouped_ggbetweenstats()
grouped_ggwithinstats()
grouped_ggscatterstats()
grouped_gghistostats()
grouped_ggbarstats()
grouped_ggpiestats()
grouped_ggcorrmat()
grouped_ggdotplotstats()

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
ggcorrmat() — Correlation Matrix
Visualises pairwise correlations across multiple continuous variables with significance annotations.

ggcorrmat(
  data   = overall_up |> select(current_age, sbp_0m, sbp_3m, sbp_6m,
                                 consumption_per_day_0m),
  title  = "Correlation Matrix — Baseline Variables",
  type   = "parametric"     # "parametric", "nonparametric", "robust", "bayes"
)

Choosing the correlation type:



type
Method
When to use




"parametric"
Pearson’s r
Continuous, approximately normal


"nonparametric"
Spearman’s ρ
Ordinal or skewed distributions


"robust"
Percentage bend r
Presence of outliers


"bayes"
Bayesian r
Quantify evidence, not just significance

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Combining with patchwork
All ggstatsplot outputs are ggplot2 objects and compose naturally with patchwork.

library(patchwork)

p1 <- ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = intervention,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  title = "Baseline SBP"
)

p2 <- ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = intervention,
  y     = sbp_3m,
  title = "3-Month SBP"
)

p3 <- ggscatterstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = sbp_0m,
  y     = sbp_3m,
  title = "Baseline vs 3-Month SBP"
)

# Compose: two plots on top, one full-width below
(p1 | p2) / p3 +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "Blood Pressure Outcomes by Intervention",
    caption = "Source: NCTOH Study Dataset"
  )

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Publication-ready output

library(ggplot2)

pub_plot <- ggbetweenstats(
  data             = overall_up,
  x                = intervention,
  y                = sbp_0m,
  type             = "parametric",
  pairwise.display = "significant",    # show only significant comparisons
  p.adjust.method  = "bonferroni",
  title            = "Baseline Systolic Blood Pressure by Intervention Group",
  xlab             = "Intervention Group",
  ylab             = "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
  package          = "RColorBrewer",
  palette          = "Set1"
) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.line        = element_line(linewidth = 0.5),
    plot.caption     = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "grey50")
  ) +
  labs(caption = "Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons shown for p < 0.05")

# Save at print quality
ggsave("figures/sbp_by_intervention.png",
       pub_plot, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)

title: ggstatsplot — Advanced
text:
Case Study: Healthcare Data
A complete example using the NCTOH study dataset — comparing the change in SBP across intervention groups, accounting for tobacco type.

library(ggstatsplot)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

# Derive SBP change variable
study_data <- overall_up |>
  mutate(sbp_change = sbp_3m - sbp_0m)

# 1. Overall change by intervention
p_overall <- ggbetweenstats(
  data  = study_data,
  x     = intervention,
  y     = sbp_change,
  type  = "parametric",
  title = "Change in SBP at 3 Months"
)

# 2. Stratified by tobacco type
p_strat <- grouped_ggbetweenstats(
  data         = study_data,
  x            = intervention,
  y            = sbp_change,
  grouping.var = tobacco_type,
  title        = "SBP Change Stratified by Tobacco Type",
  plotgrid.args = list(ncol = 3)
)

# View each
p_overall
p_strat

               bf.prior = 0.707)

                       grouping.var = stratifier)

# Correlation matrix

# Compose with patchwork

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggwithinstats() — Repeated Measures
Use this when the same participants are measured more than once (paired/within-subjects design) — for example, pre-post measurements.

library(ggstatsplot)
library(tidyr)

# Reshape from wide to long for within-subjects comparison
overall_long <- overall_up |>
  select(member_id, sbp_0m, sbp_3m) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(sbp_0m, sbp_3m),
    names_to  = "timepoint",
    values_to = "sbp"
  ) |>
  mutate(timepoint = factor(timepoint,
                            levels = c("sbp_0m", "sbp_3m"),
                            labels = c("Baseline", "3 Months")))

ggwithinstats(
  data    = overall_long,
  x       = timepoint,
  y       = sbp,
  subject.id = member_id,       # links pairs across timepoints
  title   = "Systolic BP: Baseline vs 3 Months"
)

Key differences from ggbetweenstats():

subject.id is required — it tells the function which rows are paired
Uses a paired t-test (parametric) or Wilcoxon signed-rank (non-parametric)
Lines connect paired observations in the plot

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggbarstats() — Proportions
Use this when you want to compare proportions of a categorical outcome across groups. The output includes a χ² or Fisher’s exact test.

ggbarstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,           # grouping variable (x-axis)
  y     = tobacco_type,        # outcome category (fill)
  title = "Tobacco Type by Fuel Type"
)

What the output shows:

Stacked bar chart with proportion labels
χ² test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and Cramér’s V effect size
Pairwise comparisons between bars (if > 2 groups)

Swap axes to change orientation:

# Make tobacco_type the grouping variable
ggbarstats(data = overall_up, x = tobacco_type, y = fuel_type)

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
ggpiestats() — Pie / Donut Charts
Use this for a single categorical variable, or two categorical variables where a pie chart is appropriate for the audience.

# Single variable — proportions of intervention types
ggpiestats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = intervention,
  title = "Distribution of Intervention Groups"
)


# Two variables — tobacco type by intervention
ggpiestats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = tobacco_type,
  y     = intervention,       # creates faceted pies
  title = "Tobacco Type by Intervention"
)







WarningWhen to use pie charts



Pie charts are appropriate when there are ≤ 5 categories and the audience is non-technical. For more categories or detailed comparisons, prefer ggbarstats().

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
Customising appearance
All ggstatsplot functions return a ggplot2 object, so you can extend them normally.

library(ggplot2)

ggbetweenstats(
  data        = overall_up,
  x           = fuel_type,
  y           = sbp_0m,
  # Colours for each group
  palette     = "Set2",
  package     = "RColorBrewer",
  # Remove the subtitle (statistical results) if preferred
  results.subtitle = TRUE,
  # Change point size and transparency
  point.args  = list(size = 2, alpha = 0.4),
  title       = "Systolic BP by Fuel Type"
) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  labs(caption = "Source: NCTOH Study Dataset")

Common customisation parameters:



Parameter
What it controls




palette + package
Colour palette for groups


results.subtitle
Show/hide statistical annotation


point.args
Size, alpha, shape of data points


centrality.plotting
Show/hide mean/median marker


xlab / ylab
Axis labels

title: ggstatsplot — Intermediate
text:
Introduction to Bayes Factors
When you set type = "bayes", ggstatsplot reports a Bayes Factor (BF₁₀) instead of a p-value.

ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  type  = "bayes",
  title = "Systolic BP by Fuel Type (Bayesian)"
)

Interpreting BF₁₀:



BF₁₀
Interpretation




> 100
Extreme evidence for H₁


30–100
Very strong evidence for H₁


10–30
Strong evidence for H₁


3–10
Moderate evidence for H₁


1–3
Anecdotal evidence for H₁


~1
No evidence either way


1/3–1
Anecdotal evidence for H₀


< 1/10
Strong–extreme evidence for H₀




BF₁₀ > 3: reasonably confident that H₁ (an effect exists) is supported
BF₁₀ < 1/3: reasonably confident that H₀ (no effect) is supported
Values between 1/3 and 3 are inconclusive







Note



Bayesian inference and deeper interpretation of Bayes factors is covered in ggstatsplot — Advanced.

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
Journal-Quality Documents
A well-structured YAML for a manuscript-style document:
---
title: "Effect of Clean Fuel Intervention on Blood Pressure: A Community Trial"
author:
  - name: "Dr. Mukul Maheshwari"
    affiliation: "Department of Community Medicine"
    email: "author@institution.ac.in"
  - name: "Dr. Rudresh Negi"
    affiliation: "Department of Community Medicine"
date: today
abstract: |
  **Background:** Indoor air pollution remains a major public health concern...
  **Methods:** A cluster-randomised trial was conducted...
  **Results:** ...
  **Conclusion:** ...
keywords: [indoor air pollution, blood pressure, community trial, R]
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    number-sections: true
    theme: flatly
  pdf:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
    cite-method: biblatex
    pdf-engine: xelatex
    mainfont: "Times New Roman"
    fontsize: 12pt
    geometry: "margin=2.5cm"
bibliography: references.bib
csl: vancouver.csl          # citation style (download from Zotero CSL repo)
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---

title: Quarto — Publication
Quarto — Publication
text:
Callout Blocks
Callouts draw attention to key information without disrupting text flow.
::: {.callout-note}
This is a note — useful for clarifications and asides.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Tip title
A tip with a custom heading.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
This is a warning — use for cautions about interpretation.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
Critical information the reader must not miss.
:::

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
Multi-File Quarto Projects

Books
A Quarto book renders multiple .qmd files into a single structured document (HTML, PDF, or ePub).
my-book/
├── _quarto.yml
├── index.qmd        (preface / front matter)
├── 01-intro.qmd
├── 02-methods.qmd
├── 03-results.qmd
├── 04-discussion.qmd
└── references.qmd
_quarto.yml for a book:
project:
  type: book

book:
  title: "Community Trial Methods in R"
  author: "Dr. Mukul Maheshwari"
  date: today
  chapters:
    - index.qmd
    - 01-intro.qmd
    - 02-methods.qmd
    - 03-results.qmd
    - 04-discussion.qmd
    - references.qmd

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
  pdf:
    documentclass: scrbook


Websites
For a multi-page website (like this workshop), see the project’s _quarto.yml for a working example of navbar configuration, profiles, and output directories.

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
GitHub + Quarto Publishing Workflow

Option A — Push rendered HTML to GitHub Pages

Render your project locally: quarto render
Output goes to docs/ (set output-dir: docs in _quarto.yml)
Commit and push the docs/ folder to GitHub
In your repository: Settings → Pages → Source → Branch: main, Folder: /docs

# Full publish cycle
quarto render
git add docs/
git commit -m "Rebuild site"
git push


Option B — GitHub Actions (automated rebuild)
Create .github/workflows/publish.yml:
name: Publish Quarto Site

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r-dependencies@v2
        with:
          packages: |
            any::quarto
            any::tidyverse
            any::ggstatsplot
            any::gtsummary

      - uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      - name: Render and publish
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2
        with:
          target: gh-pages
With this workflow, every push to main automatically rebuilds and deploys the site.


Option C — Quarto Pub (zero configuration)
quarto publish quarto-pub
Creates a free public site at username.quarto.pub/project-name. Suitable for sharing documents without managing a GitHub repository.

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
Embedding Shiny in Quarto
For lightweight interactivity within a static Quarto document.

Using shinylive (no server required)
shinylive compiles Shiny to WebAssembly — no Shiny server needed.
---
title: "Interactive Report"
format: html
filters:
  - shinylive
---
```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sliderInput("bins", "Bins:", 5, 50, 20),
  plotOutput("hist")
)

server <- function(input, output) {
  output$hist <- renderPlot({
    ggplot(data.frame(x = rnorm(500)), aes(x)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = input$bins)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```
Install shinylive:
install.packages("shinylive")
quarto::quarto_add_extension("quarto-ext/shinylive")


Embedding a deployed Shiny app with <iframe>
If you have an app on shinyapps.io:
<iframe src="https://yourname.shinyapps.io/yourapp/"

title: Quarto — Publication
text:
Checklist: Publication-Ready Document

YAML includes author, date, abstract, keywords
number-sections: true enabled
All figures have label: fig-* and fig-cap
All tables have label: tbl-* and tbl-cap
Cross-references used (no manual “Figure 1” text)

title: Maps and Choropleths
text: A choropleth colours each area by a value. It is the most common map in public health and also the easiest to get wrong. This page covers rates versus counts, classification, colour choice and an interactive version.

title: Maps and Choropleths
text:
Counts mislead, rates do not

p1 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_cases)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Cases") + labs(title = "Dengue cases (counts)")
p2 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "per 100,000", option = "magma", direction = -1) + labs(title = "Dengue per 100,000 (rate)")
patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)








Counts follow population size; a populous block looks bad even when its risk is average. Map rates (or standardised ratios) for risk, counts for workload.

blocks |> st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarise(r_cases_pop = cor(dengue_cases, population), r_rate_pop = cor(dengue_per_100k, population)) |> round(2)

  r_cases_pop r_rate_pop
1        0.67       0.16

title: Maps and Choropleths
text:
Classification changes the story
Continuous colour hides nothing but is hard to read; classes are easier but are a choice. Three common schemes (package classInt):

library(classInt)
cls <- function(x, style) cut(x, classIntervals(x, 5, style = style)$brks, include.lowest = TRUE)
long <- bind_rows(
  mutate(blocks, scheme = "Equal interval", cls = cls(dengue_per_100k, "equal")),
  mutate(blocks, scheme = "Quantile (equal counts)", cls = cls(dengue_per_100k, "quantile")),
  mutate(blocks, scheme = "Natural breaks (Jenks)", cls = cls(dengue_per_100k, "jenks")))
ggplot(long) + geom_sf(aes(fill = cls), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + facet_wrap(~ scheme) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "YlOrRd", name = "per 100,000") + theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text = element_blank())









Equal interval: honest about the scale, but a skewed variable puts most areas in one class.
Quantile: every class has the same number of areas, so there is always a “worst 20%” even if all are similar.
Natural breaks: groups similar values; breaks depend on the data, so maps are hard to compare.

State the scheme and the breaks in the caption. For comparing maps, use the same fixed breaks.

title: Maps and Choropleths
text:
Colour

Use a sequential palette (light to dark) for rates; a diverging palette only when there is a meaningful midpoint (e.g. ratio to the district average = 1).
Avoid rainbow palettes; check that the map reads in grey-scale and for colour-blind viewers (viridis is safe).


blocks$rr <- blocks$dengue_per_100k / (sum(blocks$dengue_cases) / sum(blocks$population) * 1e5)
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = rr)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 1, name = "Rate ratio\nvs district") +
  labs(title = "Diverging scale centred on the district rate")

title: Maps and Choropleths
section: Layers, labels and the finishing touches
text:
Layers, labels and the finishing touches

fac <- read_csv("../data/gis/facilities.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> st_as_sf(coords = c("easting_m", "northing_m"), crs = 32644) |> st_transform(4326)
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = dengue_per_100k), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = fac, aes(shape = type), size = 2) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Oranges", direction = 1, name = "Dengue per\n100,000") +
  labs(title = "Dengue incidence and health facilities", subtitle = "Synthetic district, 79 blocks", shape = "Facility") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())








Good maps carry a title, a legend with units, the data source, and a north arrow / scale bar when the area matters (ggspatial::annotation_scale() and annotation_north_arrow()).

title: Maps and Choropleths
text:
Interactive map

library(leaflet)
pal <- colorNumeric("YlOrRd", blocks$dengue_per_100k)
leaflet(blocks) |> addProviderTiles("CartoDB.Positron") |>
  addPolygons(fillColor = ~pal(dengue_per_100k), fillOpacity = 0.8, weight = 1, color = "white",
              label = ~paste0(block_name, ": ", dengue_per_100k, " per 100,000"),
              highlightOptions = highlightOptions(weight = 3, color = "black", bringToFront = TRUE)) |>
  addLegend(pal = pal, values = ~dengue_per_100k, title = "Dengue per 100,000")











Note



The synthetic district has made-up positions, so the base map shows empty countryside. With real boundaries the tiles give context.

title: Maps and Choropleths
text:
Saving

ggsave("dengue_map.png", width = 7, height = 6, dpi = 300)             # for papers
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(map, "dengue_map.html", selfcontained = TRUE)   # for the web

title: Maps and Choropleths
text:
Take-home

Map rates, not counts, unless you mean workload.
Classification is a choice: report it, and keep breaks fixed when comparing maps.
Use sequential colour for rates and diverging colour only around a meaningful midpoint.
A map can look clustered by eye; to test it, go to Neighbours and Spatial Weights and Global Moran’s I.

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
text: Moran’s I is the workhorse, but it is one of several tools. This page covers the others you will meet in papers, when each is the right one, and how to run them on the same synthetic district.

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
text:
Geary’s C
Moran’s I compares each area with the mean; Geary’s C compares neighbouring values directly (squared differences), so it is more sensitive to local differences.

C ≈ 1: no spatial autocorrelation.
C < 1: positive autocorrelation (neighbours are similar).
C > 1: negative autocorrelation.

Note the direction is opposite to Moran’s I. The two usually agree; when they disagree, look at local patterns.

geary.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)


    Geary C test under randomisation

data:  blocks$dengue_per_100k 
weights: lw   

Geary C statistic standard deviate = 7.6519, p-value = 9.903e-15
alternative hypothesis: Expectation greater than statistic
sample estimates:
Geary C statistic       Expectation          Variance 
      0.466797918       1.000000000       0.004855649

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
section: Getis-Ord General G: do high values or low values cluster?
text:
Getis-Ord General G: do high values or low values cluster?
Moran’s I cannot tell hot-spot clustering from cold-spot clustering: both give positive I. The General G can, because it sums the products of values in neighbouring pairs. Its values must be positive.

lw_b <- nb2listw(nb, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)       # G uses binary weights
globalG.test(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw_b, zero.policy = TRUE)


    Getis-Ord global G statistic

data:  blocks$dengue_per_100k 
weights: lw_b   

standard deviate = 3.0397, p-value = 0.001184
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Global G statistic        Expectation           Variance 
      7.320125e-02       6.718598e-02       3.916081e-06 


If G is above its expectation with a small p-value, high values cluster together (hot spots dominate). Below its expectation: low values cluster (cold spots).

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
text:
Join counts: binary data
For a yes/no variable (“high-burden block”), count the joins (shared borders) by type: High-High, Not-Not, and High-Not. If High areas touch each other more than expected, the pattern is clustered.

joincount.test(blocks$high_burden, lw_b, zero.policy = TRUE)


    Join count test under nonfree sampling

data:  blocks$high_burden 
weights: lw_b 

Std. deviate for Not high = 5.4811, p-value = 2.113e-08
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Same colour statistic           Expectation              Variance 
            125.00000              99.77118              21.18619 


    Join count test under nonfree sampling

data:  blocks$high_burden 
weights: lw_b 

Std. deviate for High = 6.1757, p-value = 3.294e-10
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Same colour statistic           Expectation              Variance 
             39.00000              18.54333              10.97242 


The output has one test per category. “High” joins observed above expected (positive z) means high-burden blocks are neighbours more often than chance. Use it when the variable is truly categorical, or after you have dichotomised a rate, but remember that cutting a continuous variable loses information.

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
section: Getis-Ord Gi*: hot and cold spots
text:
Getis-Ord Gi*: hot and cold spots
The local version of G gives each area a z-score from the sum of its own value and its neighbours’ (the * means the area itself is included).

nb_self <- include.self(nb)                               # the * : include the area itself
lw_self <- nb2listw(nb_self, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
blocks$gi <- as.numeric(localG(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw_self, zero.policy = TRUE))
blocks$gi_class <- cut(blocks$gi, c(-Inf, -2.58, -1.96, -1.65, 1.65, 1.96, 2.58, Inf),
                       labels = c("Cold 99%", "Cold 95%", "Cold 90%", "Not significant", "Hot 90%", "Hot 95%", "Hot 99%"))
table(blocks$gi_class)


       Cold 99%        Cold 95%        Cold 90% Not significant         Hot 90% 
              7               6               3              46               5 
        Hot 95%         Hot 99% 
              1              11 



ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = gi_class), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Cold 99%" = "#2166ac", "Cold 95%" = "#67a9cf", "Cold 90%" = "#d1e5f0", "Not significant" = "grey92",
                               "Hot 90%" = "#fddbc7", "Hot 95%" = "#ef8a62", "Hot 99%" = "#b2182b"), drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Getis-Ord Gi* hot and cold spots", subtitle = "z-score bands (|z| > 1.65, 1.96, 2.58)") + theme(legend.position = "bottom")














Note



Gi* and LISA ask different questions. LISA (local Moran) finds areas similar to their neighbours, hot or cold, plus outliers. Gi* finds where high (or low) sums concentrate, so it separates hot from cold directly but does not flag outliers. Compare the two maps; as with LISA, you ran many tests, so treat bands with the same caution (consider an FDR adjustment).

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
text:
The spatial scan statistic
Kulldorff’s scan statistic (the method behind SaTScan) moves circles of many sizes over the map and asks, for each, whether it contains more cases than expected from the population. It reports the most likely cluster and its p-value (by Monte Carlo), and any secondary clusters. It is the standard tool for disease cluster detection because it uses counts and population directly (Poisson model), so it handles different populations without first computing rates.

library(smerc)
cen_km <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_transform(blocks, 32644))) / 1000     # kilometres
set.seed(5)
sc <- scan.test(coords = cen_km, cases = blocks$dengue_cases, pop = blocks$population, nsim = 499, alpha = 0.05)
summary(sc)

  nregions max_dist cases    ex  rr stat     p
1       34     81.2   627 477.7 1.8 42.7 0.002



cl <- sc$clusters[[1]]
blocks$scan <- ifelse(seq_len(nrow(blocks)) %in% cl$locids, "Most likely cluster", "Other")
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = scan), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Most likely cluster" = "#d7191c", "Other" = "grey90"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Most likely cluster (Kulldorff scan, Poisson model)")








Read the output as: the blocks in the cluster, the observed and expected cases, the relative risk inside versus outside, and the p-value. Choose the maximum circle size (default 50% of the population) deliberately; a bigger window finds larger, more diffuse clusters.

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
text:
Which test should I use?





flowchart TD
  A[Spatial pattern question] --> B{Variable type}
  B -->|Continuous rate or measurement| C{Question}
  B -->|Yes/no or categories| J[Join counts]
  B -->|Case counts and population| S[Scan statistic]
  C -->|Is there clustering at all?| D[Moran's I, with Geary's C as check]
  C -->|Do high or low values cluster?| G[General G]
  C -->|Where are the clusters?| E{Interest}
  E -->|Clusters and outliers| L[Local Moran, LISA]
  E -->|Hot and cold spots| H[Getis-Ord Gi*]

title: Geary’s C, Getis-Ord, Join Counts and the Scan Statistic
text:
Take-home

Geary’s C (1 = none, below 1 = clustering) is a global check that reacts to local differences.
General G separates hot-spot from cold-spot clustering; Moran’s I cannot.
Join counts serve binary variables; Gi* gives hot and cold spots; the scan statistic finds the most likely cluster from counts and population.
Whatever the test, state the weights, the variable and any multiple-testing handling.
Next: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests.

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text: Ordinary regression assumes the residuals are independent. With areas, they usually are not: unexplained risk is shared between neighbours. This breaks standard errors, and the usual diagnostic is Moran’s I on the residuals. This page runs the whole workflow.

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
1. Fit the ordinary model

ols <- lm(dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct, data = blocks)
summary(ols)$coefficients |> round(3)

              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   -101.067     61.802  -1.635    0.106
poverty_index    1.445      0.335   4.306    0.000
literacy_pct     0.981      0.603   1.629    0.107

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
section: 2. Test the residuals for spatial autocorrelation
text:
2. Test the residuals for spatial autocorrelation

lm.morantest(ols, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)


    Global Moran I for regression residuals

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
weights: lw

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 4.4335, p-value = 4.635e-06
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Observed Moran I      Expectation         Variance 
     0.273945405     -0.023128244      0.004489825 


A significant, positive Moran’s I of the residuals means the model leaves spatial structure unexplained: the independence assumption fails, and standard errors are probably too small.

blocks$res_ols <- residuals(ols)
ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = res_ols)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", name = "Residual") + labs(title = "OLS residuals: neighbouring blocks share the same sign")

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
section: 3. Which spatial model? Lagrange multiplier tests
text:
3. Which spatial model? Lagrange multiplier tests
Two common spatial structures:








Model
Idea
Equation (sketch)




Spatial lag (SAR)
my outcome depends on my neighbours’ outcomes (spillover, contagion)
\(y = \rho W y + X\beta + \varepsilon\)


Spatial error (SEM)
unmeasured shared factors make neighbouring errors alike
\(y = X\beta + u,\; u = \lambda W u + \varepsilon\)



The LM tests and their robust versions help choose:

lm.RStests(ols, lw, test = c("RSerr", "RSlag", "adjRSerr", "adjRSlag"), zero.policy = TRUE)


    Rao's score (a.k.a Lagrange multiplier) diagnostics for spatial
    dependence

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
test weights: lw

RSerr = 14.895, df = 1, p-value = 0.0001137


    Rao's score (a.k.a Lagrange multiplier) diagnostics for spatial
    dependence

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
test weights: lw

RSlag = 19.289, df = 1, p-value = 1.124e-05


    Rao's score (a.k.a Lagrange multiplier) diagnostics for spatial
    dependence

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
test weights: lw

adjRSerr = 0.15191, df = 1, p-value = 0.6967


    Rao's score (a.k.a Lagrange multiplier) diagnostics for spatial
    dependence

data:  
model: lm(formula = dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct,
data = blocks)
test weights: lw

adjRSlag = 4.5459, df = 1, p-value = 0.033


Rule of thumb: if both RSerr and RSlag are significant, prefer the model whose robust test (adjRSerr or adjRSlag) is larger and significant. If only one is, use that. Use theory as well: contagion points to lag, omitted shared exposures to error.

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
4. Fit the spatial models

library(spatialreg)
sem <- errorsarlm(dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct, data = blocks, listw = lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
sar <- lagsarlm(dengue_per_100k ~ poverty_index + literacy_pct, data = blocks, listw = lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
summary(sem)$Coef |> round(3)

              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)    -39.286     53.414  -0.736    0.462
poverty_index    0.956      0.344   2.779    0.005
literacy_pct     0.513      0.512   1.002    0.316

c(lambda = sem$lambda, rho = sar$rho) |> round(3)

lambda.lambda       rho.rho 
        0.535         0.515 


lambda (error model) and rho (lag model) measure the spatial dependence; their likelihood-ratio tests (in the model summary()) say whether it is needed.

tibble(model = c("OLS", "Spatial error", "Spatial lag"), AIC = c(AIC(ols), AIC(sem), AIC(sar))) |> mutate(AIC = round(AIC, 1))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  model           AIC
  <chr>         <dbl>
1 OLS            698.
2 Spatial error  687.
3 Spatial lag    685.


The lower the AIC the better; compare them on the same data.

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
5. Check the residuals again

moran.test(residuals(sem), lw, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1] |> round(3)

Moran I statistic 
           -0.042 

moran.test(residuals(ols), lw, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1] |> round(3)

Moran I statistic 
            0.274 


If the residual Moran’s I has dropped close to its expectation (about 0), the model has absorbed the spatial structure.

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
6. Interpreting coefficients: a warning

In the error model the coefficients keep the OLS meaning (change in rate per unit of the covariate), but with corrected standard errors.
In the lag model a change in a block’s covariate also changes neighbours’ outcomes, which feed back. The coefficient is not the total effect; use impacts (direct, indirect and total):


set.seed(6)
imp <- impacts(sar, listw = lw, R = 199)
summary(imp, zstats = TRUE, short = TRUE)

Impact measures (lag, exact):
                       Direct  Indirect    Total
poverty_index dy/dx 0.9339023 0.8647157 1.798618
literacy_pct dy/dx  0.8134276 0.7531661 1.566594
========================================================
Simulation results ( variance matrix):
========================================================
Simulated standard errors
                       Direct  Indirect     Total
poverty_index dy/dx 0.3400153 0.5790857 0.7998079
literacy_pct dy/dx  0.6010227 0.8975023 1.4072140

Simulated z-values:
                      Direct  Indirect    Total
poverty_index dy/dx 2.715598 1.5611009 2.284744
literacy_pct dy/dx  1.332292 0.9089538 1.148742

Simulated p-values:
                    Direct    Indirect Total   
poverty_index dy/dx 0.0066156 0.11850  0.022328
literacy_pct dy/dx  0.1827641 0.36337  0.250662

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
Other routes

Add covariates that explain the clustering (poverty here may not be the only driver); if the residual autocorrelation vanishes you may not need a spatial model.
Mixed models with a spatial random effect (CAR/BYM in INLA or brms) are the standard for small-area disease mapping with count data and different populations.
Geographically weighted regression lets coefficients vary over space.

title: Spatial Regression and Residual Tests
text:
Take-home

Always test the residuals of a regression on areas, with lm.morantest().
LM tests (and their robust versions) suggest lag or error; theory should agree.
Report the spatial parameter (rho or lambda), compare AIC with OLS, re-check the residuals, and use impacts for the lag model.
For counts and unequal populations, look at Poisson models with spatial random effects.

title: Spatial Statistics Cheat Sheet
text:
Question
Variable
Test
R




Is the map clustered?
continuous
Moran’s I
moran.test() / moran.mc()


Same, check from another angle
continuous
Geary’s C
geary.test()


Do high (or low) values cluster?
continuous, positive
General G
globalG.test() (binary weights)


Do same-category areas touch?
yes/no, categories
Join counts
joincount.test()


Where are clusters and outliers?
continuous
Local Moran (LISA)
localmoran()


Where are hot and cold spots?
continuous, positive
Getis-Ord Gi*
localG() + include.self()


Most likely cluster from counts and population
counts + population
Scan statistic
smerc::scan.test()


Are regression residuals spatially independent?
residuals
Moran on residuals
lm.morantest()


Lag or error model?
residuals
LM tests
lm.RStests()













Result
Meaning




I ≈ 0 (E[I] = −1/(n−1))
no spatial pattern


I clearly > 0, small p
clustering: similar values are neighbours


I clearly < 0
dispersion (checkerboard)



Our synthetic district: I = 0.50, E[I] = -0.013, p < 0.001. Geary’s C = 0.47 (C < 1 = clustering: opposite direction to I). Prefer the permutation p (moran.mc, 999 simulations: smallest p = 0.001).











Neighbours
spdep
Use for




Queen / rook contiguity
poly2nb(queen = TRUE/FALSE)
polygons of similar size


k nearest
knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k))
unequal areas, points


Distance band

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Where we are

Session 1: spatial data, CRS, joins, honest maps
Every spatial test asks: are neighbouring areas more alike than chance?
First we must define “neighbour”. That definition is the spatial weights matrix, the most influential choice in the analysis
By the end you can:

build queen, rook, k-nearest and distance neighbours
turn them into row-standardised weights
compute and read a spatial lag
check how sensitive a result is to the choice

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
Contiguity: share a boundary



Rook: share an edge
Queen: share an edge or a corner (the usual default)
Needs polygons; areas of similar size behave best
Watch for islands: areas with no neighbour



nb_q <- poly2nb(blocks, queen = TRUE,  snap = 1e-4)
nb_r <- poly2nb(blocks, queen = FALSE, snap = 1e-4)
c(queen_links = sum(card(nb_q)), rook_links = sum(card(nb_r)))

queen_links  rook_links 
        414         414

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
section: A neighbour list says who; weights say how much
text:
A neighbour list says who; weights say how much







Style
Meaning




"B" binary
1 for every neighbour


"W" row-standardised
each area’s weights sum to 1; the usual choice


"S"
variance-stabilising




lw <- nb2listw(nb_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
lw$weights[[1]]

[1] 0.25 0.25 0.25 0.25

sum(lw$weights[[1]])

[1] 1



With "W", area i gives each of its k neighbours weight 1/k. An area with 2 neighbours weights each by 0.5; one with 8 by 0.125.

title: Session 2 — Neighbours and Spatial Weights
text:
The spatial lag

lag(x)i = Σj wij xj = the average of i’s neighbours

p2 <- ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = lag_rate)) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, name = NULL) + labs(title = "Spatial lag (neighbours' average)")

One statistic per area

loc <- localmoran(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
head(round(loc, 3), 4)

Column
Meaning

this area’s local I: > 0 similar to neighbours, < 0 unlike them


Z.Ii

Pr(z != E(Ii))
two-sided p-value




The average of the local values equals the global I: the global statistic is the average of the local ones (0.499).

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text:
Multiple testing
You ran 79 tests: at 5%, about 4 blocks look significant by chance, and the tests are correlated (neighbours share neighbours).

c(unadjusted = sum(p < 0.05), fdr = sum(p.adjust(p, "fdr") < 0.05), bonferroni = sum(p.adjust(p, "bonferroni") < 0.05))

unadjusted        fdr bonferroni 
        22         13          3 



FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg) is a sensible default; Bonferroni is the strictest
Treat LISA as exploratory: it tells you where to look
The analytic p-values assume near-normal data; localmoran_perm() gives permutation p-values for skewed rates

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text:
Hot and cold spots directly
Gi* sums the values of an area and its neighbours (the * includes the area itself) and turns the sum into a z-score.

lw_self <- nb2listw(include.self(nb), style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
blocks$gi <- as.numeric(localG(blocks$dengue_per_100k, lw_self, zero.policy = TRUE))
blocks$gi_class <- cut(blocks$gi, c(-Inf, -2.58, -1.96, -1.65, 1.65, 1.96, 2.58, Inf),
                       labels = c("Cold 99%", "Cold 95%", "Cold 90%", "Not significant", "Hot 90%", "Hot 95%", "Hot 99%"))
table(blocks$gi_class)


       Cold 99%        Cold 95%        Cold 90% Not significant         Hot 90% 
              7               6               3              46               5 
        Hot 95%         Hot 99% 
              1              11 



ggplot(blocks) + geom_sf(aes(fill = gi_class), colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Cold 99%" = "#2166ac", "Cold 95%" = "#67a9cf", "Cold 90%" = "#d1e5f0", "Not significant" = "grey92",
                               "Hot 90%" = "#fddbc7", "Hot 95%" = "#ef8a62", "Hot 99%" = "#b2182b"), drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Getis-Ord Gi* hot and cold spots")

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text:
Gi* or LISA?

LISA finds areas similar to their neighbours (hot or cold) and outliers.


Gi* finds where high (or low) sums concentrate: it separates hot from cold directly, but does not flag outliers.


Both run one test per area: apply the same multiple-testing caution.

title: Session 4 — Local Clusters and Hot Spots
text:
Kulldorff’s circles
Slide circles of many sizes over the map; for each ask whether it holds more cases than expected from the population. Reports the most likely cluster, its relative risk and a Monte Carlo p-value. Uses counts and population (Poisson), so no rates are needed.

cen_km <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_transform(blocks, 32644))) / 1000
set.seed(5)
sc <- scan.test(coords = cen_km, cases = blocks$dengue_cases, pop = blocks$population, nsim = 499, alpha = 0.05)
summary(sc)

  nregions max_dist cases    ex  rr stat     p
1       34     81.2   627 477.7 1.8 42.7 0.002



Read: blocks in the cluster, observed vs expected cases, relative risk, p-value
The maximum window (default 50% of the population) changes what you find; choose it deliberately
Report the model (Poisson), the window, the number of simulations
